theme: an aria-live/role=status container is created in the very same render as the text it first announces, instead of already existing in the DOM before the content changes
summary: The zero-match message (`Nobody matches "…"`) is wrapped in a `role="status" aria-live="polite"` div that only exists in the DOM when `open && matches.length === 0` — so on the exact keystroke that first produces zero matches (e.g. typing a name nobody has), the region and its text appear in the same commit, the same anti-pattern Notice.tsx was built to avoid.
failure: Type a query that matches nobody on the very first character that empties the result set: the announcement of "Nobody matches…" is not guaranteed to be spoken because the live region did not exist a render earlier.
remediation: Render the `search-empty` status div unconditionally alongside the input (empty string when there are matches or the query is empty) instead of gating its mount on `open && matches.length === 0`.
invariant: Every element carrying `aria-live`/`role="status"` must already exist in a DOM commit prior to the render that first supplies its non-empty announced text.

theme: the focus rescue's `??` anchor fallback never engages when the primary anchor is present-but-unfocusable, so a reopened dialog can leave keyboard focus silently stranded
summary: `useFocusRescue`'s anchor is `searchRef.current ?? document.querySelector('[aria-label="Roster names"]')`. Clicking "Edit people" while a graph is on screen sets `modalOpen = true`, which makes `#app` (and therefore the still-mounted `PersonSearch` input `searchRef` points at) `inert` in the same commit. `??` only falls through when the left side is `null`/`undefined` — but `searchRef.current` is a real, non-null DOM node, just one that is now inside an inert subtree, so the fallback to the roster textarea is never tried. Per spec, calling `.focus()` on an element inside an `inert` subtree is a no-op, so `useFocusRescue`'s `target.focus()` call silently fails, `document.activeElement` stays `<body>`, and `hadFocus.current` is left `true` waiting for a commit that (in this flow) never comes. This contradicts the hook's own documented guarantee ("Put focus back somewhere usable whenever a render destroys the focused element") and is invisible to the existing test suite, which explicitly notes jsdom does not implement inert's focus-blocking behaviour (`app/test/appErrorRecovery.test.tsx:183`), so a jsdom-based assertion of `document.activeElement` after this flow would pass even though real browsers fail it.
failure: With a graph on screen, Tab to "Edit people" and press Enter: in a real browser, focus is dropped to `<body>` instead of being rescued into the reopened RosterModal's textarea. The user recovers only by pressing Tab once more (relying on `#app`'s inertness removing its contents from the tab order) rather than via the rescue mechanism that exists specifically to avoid making them do that.
remediation: Have the anchor function check focusability (e.g. `el.closest('[inert]') === null`) before returning `searchRef.current`, or have `useFocusRescue` itself verify `document.activeElement === target` after calling `.focus()` and retry the anchor chain (not just the same anchor) on failure.
invariant: `useFocusRescue`'s anchor resolution must never treat a present-but-currently-unfocusable element (e.g. one inside an `inert` subtree) as a successful target; if the primary candidate cannot actually receive focus, resolution must continue to the next candidate rather than stopping on it.

theme: Function parameter name describes how (degree in general) rather than what (actual vs. target)
summary: quality() function parameter k is semantically actual degree but named ambiguously
failure: A maintainer unfamiliar with the Moore bound context might call quality(aspl, n, settings.buddies) intending to score against target k, when it requires actual degreeMax. The single call site is correct (line 236), but the definition is unclear for new callers.
remediation: Rename parameter from `k` to `actualDegree` or `degreeMax`, or add to the docstring: 'k: the actual measured degree of this graph (degreeMax), used to compute Moore bound score'.
invariant: quality(aspl, n, d) is called only when d is the measured maximum degree of the graph, never a target k or average degree. Equivalently: d == raw.degreeMax when called from assembleMetrics, and never d == settings.buddies or d == n.

theme: Function relies on implicit invariant (bound on degree) enforced elsewhere, not documented as contract
summary: neighborhood() assumes all degrees <= BUDDY_MAX but this is not documented as a precondition
failure: The function comment on line 10 mentions the bound as justification for algorithm choice (O(k²) instead of BFS), not as a contract. If a future code path creates graphs from an untrusted source without the importGraph checks, this assumption could be violated and neighborhood() would silently compute wrong results. The O(k²) loop assumes degree[focus] and degree[buddies] are each at most 12; violating this makes the span up to n² without comment.
remediation: Add explicit precondition to neighborhood() docstring: 'Requires: all adjacency lists have length <= BUDDY_MAX (12). Used only after graph creation ensures this bound.' Alternatively, add an assertion in the function body to make violations fail loudly rather than silently.
invariant: For any adjacency list passed to neighborhood(), all vertices have degree <= BUDDY_MAX. This is currently enforced by importGraph.ts line 262-265 (rejects degreeMax > BUDDY_MAX) and generation (k capped to BUDDY_MAX), but not formalized as a documented requirement.

theme: a focused button's visible label is used as the only signal of a transient state change, with no accompanying live region, unlike the identical pattern elsewhere in the same codebase
summary: The Copy button's own text flips between "Copy" and "Copied" for 1.1s after activation, with no `aria-live`/`role="status"` anywhere near it. `SettingsControls.tsx` solves the structurally identical problem (a button that keeps focus after a press, whose only visible feedback is a value that changed) by wrapping the changed value in a separate `role="status" aria-live="polite"` span, with a comment explaining that relying on the focused control's own label change is not enough ("the buttons keep focus, so without it a screen-reader user pressing '+' hears nothing at all"). BuddyList's Copy button does not follow that established fix.
failure: Activate Copy from the keyboard: whether "Copied" is announced depends on the AT/browser combination re-announcing a focused button's changed accessible name, which `SettingsControls`'s own comment treats as not reliable enough to depend on for the same UI shape.
remediation: Add a small `role="status" aria-live="polite"` sibling (visually hidden if desired) next to the Copy button that announces "Copied" on success, mirroring `SettingsControls`'s stepper pattern.
invariant: Every control whose only feedback is a change to its own accessible name while it keeps focus must expose that change via an adjacent `aria-live`/`role="status"` element (as `SettingsControls`'s stepper already does), not rely on re-announcement of the focused element's label alone.

theme: the identical-graph short-circuit keeps stale fields from the previous view, so the UI reports state the core has already superseded
summary: The identical-graph short-circuit adopts settings, constraints AND report, but its `changed` predicate tests only settings and constraints — so a freshly computed ConstraintReport is discarded whenever the regenerated graph is byte-identical and the rules/settings are unchanged.
failure: Generate an 8-person graph with rules [{0,4 required},{1,2 prohibited}] at k=3 → export → import (view.report === null, panel reads "2 buddy rules saved with this graph — not re-checked on import.") → "Edit people" → Generate with nothing changed. Generation is deterministic and export/import is exact, so sameStrings+sameEdges hold and sameSettings+sameConstraints both return true ⇒ changed === false ⇒ setView is never called. view.report stays null and QualityPanel still says "not re-checked on import" even though buildConstrainedBuddyGraph just ran and returned a report with reqViolations=0/prohViolations=0. Reproduced in .review-scratch/mine/report.probe.tsx (assertion `expect(v.report).not.toBeNull()` fails). The existing suite does not cover this path.
remediation: Stop predicting which adopted fields changed. Either drop the `changed` guard and always `setView({...cur, settings: next.settings, constraints: next.constraints, report: next.report})` in the identical branch (React bails out on an equal-by-value re-render anyway, and the point of the branch is only to preserve the `edges`/`buddies` identities), or — if the guard must stay — derive it from the same set of fields it adopts (add `cur.report !== next.report`). Fixing only `report` leaves the sibling open the moment a fourth field is adopted.
invariant: For every generation result the effect consumes, the resulting view's `report` is identical to that result's `report` (`view.report === consumedResult.report`); no view field that the identical-graph branch adopts may ever retain a value inherited from a previous view.

theme: a rule row the user has not finished typing is reported as a broken rule, and the row-level and summary-level validity checks disagree about the empty string
summary: `resolveNamedPairs` looks up `""` like any other name, so a still-empty (or half-filled) rule row is counted under `unmatched` and RosterModal immediately claims it "names someone who isn't in this roster" — while ConstraintsEditor's own `unknownName` explicitly exempts empty text and leaves the row unflagged.
failure: Open the roster modal on any roster and click "+ Add a buddy rule" once, typing nothing. The row's inputs have value "" and no `aria-invalid` (the row says it is fine), but the modal renders "1 buddy rule names someone who isn't in this roster and won't be used." `resolveNamedPairs([{a:"Alice",b:"",kind:"required"}], roster)` likewise returns `unmatched: 1`. Reproduced in .review-scratch/mine/editor.probe.tsx. The one existing assertion on this string (test/constraintsFlow.test.tsx:91) uses a genuinely unknown name, so the suite is blind to the blank case.
remediation: Give `resolveNamedPairs` an `incomplete` cause for rows whose `a` or `b` is empty after trimming, and count them there instead of under `unmatched` (report them with copy about finishing the row, or not at all). That makes the summary's per-cause counts and `ConstraintsEditor`'s per-row `aria-invalid` derive from one definition of "names nobody" — the same definition `resolvePerson` already uses when it returns -1 for empty text.
invariant: For every rows list and roster, `resolveNamedPairs(rows, names).unmatched` counts a row only if at least one of its post-trim NON-EMPTY fields fails to resolve; equivalently, for every row the summary attributes a resolution failure to it iff `ConstraintsEditor` marks that row `aria-invalid`.

theme: a sentence whose truth depends on a builder having run is rendered unconditionally, so it makes a false causal claim about imported graphs
summary: `targetShortfall` compares `settings.buddies` against `metrics.degreeMax` with no regard for how the view was produced, so QualityPanel renders "You asked for N buddies each; this roster only allows M" for imported edge sets no generator ever built — blaming the roster for a limit that comes from the file.
failure: Import {version:1, people:[A..F], edges: 6-cycle, settings:{buddies:4,...}}: `targetShortfall` returns {asked:4, got:2} and QualityPanel displays "You asked for 4 buddies each; this roster only allows 2." A 6-person roster plainly allows 4 buddies each — the file's sparse edge list is the limit, and the user never "asked" for anything on this path. Second reachable form: import {people:[A,B], edges:[[0,1]]} with no settings block; `sanitizeSettings` synthesises `buddies: 2` via the BUDDY_MIN clamp, producing {asked:2, got:1} and the same sentence about a request that was never made. Both reproduced in .review-scratch/mine/shortfall.probe.tsx.
remediation: Fix it by subtraction in the copy rather than by adding provenance state: word the line about the graph instead of the roster and the request (e.g. "Each person has M buddies, not the N in Settings"), which is true on both the generation and the import path. If the "you asked / the roster allows" framing is worth keeping, it needs an explicit origin marker on GraphView and must be suppressed for imported views — and the synthesised `buddies` from the BUDDY_MIN clamp must not feed it either, or the sibling stays open.
invariant: No copy derived from `targetShortfall` may attribute the delivered degree to the ROSTER or to a user request for a view no builder produced: for every imported view, the quality panel renders no text matching /this roster only allows/ and no "you asked for" claim unless the file declared that buddy count.

theme: roster content of attacker-chosen size is rendered into the setup dialog with no length clamp, and the dialog cannot be scrolled or dismissed once it overflows
summary:
`parseRoster`'s de-duplication warning enumerates EVERY de-duplicated name by hand (`[...extras.keys()].map(...).join(", ")`). `extras` is bounded only by MAX_NAMES-1 (999) and each name by MAX_NAME_CHARS (120), so one warning string reaches ~122 KB. RosterModal renders `parsed.warnings` straight into `
{w}
` with no clamp — `useNotice.clampNotice` (MAX_NOTICE_CHARS=300) guards the toast, not this sink. `.note` has no max-height, `.sheet` has no max-height, and `#modal` is `position:fixed` flex-centered with `overflow: visible`, so the note's height is added to a centered box and pushes the top of the sheet off-screen with nothing scrollable to bring it back.
failure: Drop (or paste) a .txt roster of 999 distinct 120-character names, each listed twice — 241,757 characters, comfortably inside the 8 MB file gate and the 500,000-char MAX_PARSE_CHARS cap. Measured in headless Chromium against `app/dist`: the warning is 121,935 characters, its `.note` box is 15,015 px tall, `.sheet` becomes 15,521 px tall with `top: -7310`, and the roster textarea (`top: -7168`) and the "Generate buddy graph" button (`top: -6910`) are both ABOVE the viewport. `document.documentElement.scrollHeight` is 900 (= innerHeight), so there is no scrollbar; `#modal` computed `overflow` is `visible`. `ta.focus(); ta.scrollIntoView()` leaves `top` at -7182 with `scrollY` 0 — the controls stay unreachable. On first load `canCancel` is false so there is no Cancel button, and `useEscape` is suspended while the modal is open, so nothing on screen is interactive and the only recovery is a page reload. Each further keystroke re-renders the 122 KB node (78-82 ms).
remediation: Bound the enumeration where it is built: list at most a fixed number of de-duplicated names and end with "and N more" (the same shape `PersonPanel`'s SECOND_LIMIT already uses), so the warning length is constant. Then close the amplifier as defence in depth by clamping at the render sink too — reuse `clampNotice` for `.note` text, since per-site truncation cannot be enforced mechanically and `useNotice` already documents exactly that argument.
invariant: For every input string s, every element of `parseRoster(s).warnings` has length <= a fixed constant (the same MAX_NOTICE_CHARS the toast sink already uses) — the bound must not depend on s.length, on how many names were de-duplicated, or on how long those names are. Mechanically checkable as a property test over arbitrary s.

theme: a pasted search query is echoed verbatim into a rendered aria-live region with no length clamp, so its layout cost is unbounded in the paste size
summary: `{open && matches.length === 0 ? `Nobody matches “${query.trim()}”` : ""}` interpolates the entire query into `.search-empty`. The input has no `maxLength`, `query` is never capped (unlike the roster textarea, which `RosterModal.capText` pre-caps to MAX_PARSE_CHARS), and `.search-empty` is a VISIBLE element (`padding: 8px; font-size: 12px`) inside `#search { position: absolute; width: 240px }` with no `max-height`, no `overflow`, and no `white-space: nowrap` (unlike `.sr-live`, which does have nowrap). So a paste wraps into hundreds of thousands of line boxes inside a 240 px column, synchronously, on the main thread — and the region is `aria-live="polite"`, so a screen reader is additionally handed the whole string to announce.
failure: Paste a 4,000,000-character string into the "Find a person" box. Measured in headless Chromium against the built `app/dist` (roster = the example names, so `#search` is mounted): 3,766 ms from input event to painted frame, `.search-empty` text length 4,000,016, element height 1,363,666 px. At 1 MB it is 622 ms / 340,936 px; the cost is linear in the paste, so a 20 MB clipboard (trivially available) is ~19 s. Every subsequent keystroke re-does the whole layout. Confirmed independently in jsdom that the component itself is the producer: a 4 MB `fireEvent.change` yields a 4,000,017-character text node in the `aria-live="polite"` region.
remediation: Clamp the echoed query at the interpolation (reuse the same truncate-with-ellipsis helper as `clampNotice`/`quote` rather than adding a fourth ad-hoc one) and put a `maxLength` on the search input so the state itself cannot hold a multi-megabyte string. Adding `white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis` to `.search-empty` is worth doing too but is not the fix — it caps the line boxes, not the text node or what the live region announces.
invariant: For every value of `query`, the length of the text rendered into `.search-empty` is <= a fixed constant independent of `query.length`. More generally: no DOM text node the app renders may have a length that grows with an unbounded user input — the three clamps that exist (`clampNotice` 300, `importGraph.quote` 80, `capText` MAX_PARSE_CHARS) must cover every render sink, not three of them.

theme: the setup dialog has no overflow guard, so any oversized content permanently strands its controls off-screen
summary: `#modal { position: fixed; inset: 0; display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center; }` with `.sheet { width: min(560px, 92vw); padding: 28px; }` — neither has `max-height` or `overflow`. Because the sheet is centre-aligned in a fixed, non-scrolling container, any content taller than the viewport is clipped SYMMETRICALLY: half of it goes above `top: 0`, where neither a scrollbar nor `scrollIntoView` can reach it. This is the amplifier that turns the parseRoster warning above from jank into an unrecoverable dialog, and it is independent of that particular producer — the `<details>` rules block at the 200-rule cap, or `ruleProblems` rendering a few hundred blocking notes, reach the same state. Filed separately because clamping one producer does not close the class, and the dialog is modal: `#app` is `inert` behind it, first-run has no Cancel, and `useEscape` is suspended while it is open.
failure: Same reproduction as the parseRoster finding: with a 121,935-character note the sheet is 15,521 px tall at `top: -7310`; `#modal` computed `overflow` is `visible`, `document.documentElement.scrollHeight` equals `innerHeight` (900), and `textarea.focus(); textarea.scrollIntoView()` leaves it at `top: -7182` with `scrollY` 0. No control is on screen and no gesture brings one back.
remediation: Give the dialog an overflow guard: `#modal { overflow: auto; align-items: flex-start; }` with vertical padding, or `.sheet { max-height: calc(100vh - 32px); overflow: auto; }`. Either makes the sheet's own content scrollable so no amount of note/rule content can put a control out of reach, independently of whatever produced the content.
invariant: For every content the roster dialog can render, the roster textarea and the "Generate buddy graph" button either have a client rect inside the viewport, or have a scrollable ancestor whose `scrollHeight > clientHeight` that can bring them into view. Checkable in a browser harness by asserting `getBoundingClientRect().top >= 0` for both controls after `scrollIntoView()`.

theme: F9 (minimal-disruption recalc / 'preserve current buddies') has no representation anywhere in the app's constraint model, worker protocol, or RosterModal props, and building it would fan out across several files that currently have no notion of a prior
summary: Independently traced (not just re-read) the fan-out F9 requires: ConstraintKind ('required'|'prohibited') would need a third concept for priors, but priors are structurally different from the user-typed rows ConstraintsEditor/NamedPair model (derived from the PREVIOUS view's edges rather than typed by the user), so naively adding a 'prior' variant to ConstraintKind would leak into the manual rule editor's KIND_LABEL/select UI where it doesn't belong. Separately, worker/protocol.ts's GenerateRequest/GenerateOptions carry no priorWeight/priorHard field even though the core (lib/src/core/constraints.ts addPrior/priorHard, index.ts priorWeight) already supports it, and RosterModal — the only 'Edit people' surface — receives only names/settings/rules from App.tsx, never view.edges, so there is no data source in scope to derive priors from at the toggle's natural UI location.
failure: n/a - no caller exists yet; mechanically confirmed via grep -rn 'priorWeight|priorHard|addPrior|ConstraintKind' app/src, which returns only the required/prohibited machinery and zero prior references
remediation: When F9 is scheduled: (1) pass the live view (or at least view.edges + view.names) into RosterModal from App.tsx; (2) add a name-keyed prior-derivation analogous to resolveNamedPairs but sourced from previous edges, not typed rows; (3) extend GenerateOptions with priorWeight/priorHard and thread it through worker/generate.ts's toConstraints call (cons.addPrior/cons.priorHard), kept independent of ConstraintPair/ConstraintKind so it never surfaces in ConstraintsEditor's UI.
invariant: for every exported name in lib/src/core's prior API (addPrior, priorHard, priorWeight, priorsKeptFraction), grep -rn '<name>' app/src returns at least one caller once F9 ships; until then it returns none, which is the mechanical no-caller test this finding is filed against

theme: Feature label mismatch - comment describes deferred feature under wrong feature number
summary: Comments refer to 'F8 focus' as a future feature, but F8 is actually 'fuzzy search, clickable panel names, and a working back stack' per CLAUDE.md. The focus/ego layout is a separate, deferred feature (DEFERRED PAST M3).
failure: A developer reading lines 26-27 and 40-41 will believe F8 is the focus/ego layout. In reality: PersonSearch (F8), PersonPanel (F8), useExplorerHistory (F8) are already being built. The layout-mode they refer to is unrelated to F8.
remediation: Replace 'F8 focus' with 'a future selection-dependent mode' OR update to: 'A future SELECTION-DEPENDENT mode (not F8 — focus/ego layout is deferred past M3) whose points move per hover/click'
invariant: Comments naming a feature number X must match X's acceptance criteria in app/CLAUDE.md

theme: the app's single focus-rescue mechanism has a fixed, incomplete list of fallback anchors, so a commit that strands focus on <body> outside those anchors' reach is not actually rescued despite the mechanism's stated purpose
summary: When the FIRST generation is dispatched (RosterModal's 'Generate buddy graph' button, which has focus, is unmounted the same commit that sets bg.status to 'running' and makes #app inert), useFocusRescue's anchor function has no reachable candidate: searchRef is inside the now-inert #app, and the roster-names textarea no longer exists because the modal just closed. Focus is left on <body> even though the busy overlay's Cancel button — the only non-inert, visible, interactive element on screen — is sitting right there and was explicitly called out in App.tsx's own comment as the reason the rescue mechanism needed the overlay treated as a sibling of #app.
failure: Reproduced with a scratch RTL test: render <App/>, focus the 'Generate buddy graph' button, click it (worker mocked to report status='running'). After the commit, document.activeElement === document.body while document.querySelector('.busy button') (the Cancel button) is present, visible, and not inert — but never received focus. A screen-reader/keyboard-only user who just triggered generation has no accessible cue where focus went; they must blindly press Tab once and hope, rather than the rescue landing them on Cancel the way it lands on the search box or the roster textarea in every other traced transition.
remediation: Add a third fallback in App.tsx's useFocusRescue anchor — e.g. a ref on the busy overlay's Cancel button, tried after searchRef and the roster-names field — so the anchor resolves to a real focusable element whenever bg.status === 'running' regardless of whether the transition came from a first generation (modal→overlay) or a reroll (rail button→overlay, where a real browser's inert-triggered blur produces the identical dead end, though jsdom cannot simulate that half of the repro).
invariant: Whenever document.activeElement becomes document.body immediately after a React commit that had focus somewhere real beforehand (the exact condition useFocusRescue's own hadFocus/activeElement check gates on), the anchor function must resolve to a non-null, non-inert, mounted, focusable element for every value of bg.status/modalOpen the app can be in — including status==='running' after the setup modal has already closed.

theme: text that appears or disappears in response to user input must live inside a region that already exists in the accessibility tree before the change, or the change is invisible to a non-visual user — the app applies this discipline everywhere except RosterModal
summary: RosterModal renders six distinct kinds of dynamically-appearing validation text with zero aria-live/role=status/role=alert anywhere in the component: fileError (a rejected .txt/.csv drop or file-picker choice), inputCapped (character-cap truncation), parsed.warnings (roster-parse notes, e.g. duplicate names), feas.messages (the buddy-count feasibility gate — the one that also disables the Generate button), resolved.unmatched/selfPair/duplicate (buddy-rule resolution notes), and ruleProblems (the buddy-rule feasibility gate). Every one of these recomputes live via useMemo off `text`/`settings`/`rules` on every keystroke or stepper press, so a message can appear or vanish on literally every interaction — silently, to anyone not looking at the screen. This is the exact 'silence is indistinguishable from a broken box' failure mode the rest of the app (busy-live, sr-live, the toast, PersonSearch's search-empty region, SettingsControls' stepper role=status) was explicitly hardened against; RosterModal — the very first screen on cold load, and the one the app reopens on every refusal/error — was missed.
failure: A screen-reader user raises the 'Buddies each' stepper past what the roster supports (or pastes a roster that trips a parse warning, or drops an unreadable file). The Generate button silently becomes disabled — no aria-disabled reason, no aria-describedby to the message explaining why — and the explanatory note (`feas.messages`, rendered as a plain non-live <div>) is never announced. The user has no accessible signal that anything changed; they must independently rediscover the note by manually re-reading the whole modal, which nothing prompts them to do. Confirmed by grep: `aria-live` does not appear anywhere in RosterModal.tsx, versus five other components in the same codebase that use exactly this pattern for an analogous problem.
remediation: Wrap the note stack (or at minimum feas.messages/ruleProblems, which gate the primary action) in a permanently-mounted role='status' aria-live='polite' region, following the same pattern already used by App.tsx's busy-live/sr-live, Notice.tsx's toast-region, and PersonSearch's search-empty region — the region exists in the DOM from first render; only its text content changes.
invariant: For every text node in RosterModal whose presence/content is a function of `text`, `settings`, `rules`, or file-read results (i.e. every note derived via useMemo from those in RosterModal.tsx), that text must be rendered inside an element that carries aria-live (directly or via an always-mounted ancestor) — a validation message must never be the sole content of a div that is only conditionally present in the tree.

theme: the sequence in which panels receive focus on Tab does not track their position on screen, so a sighted keyboard user's focus jumps unpredictably between screen regions instead of moving in one direction
summary: Traced JSX render order against each panel's CSS position: DOM/tab order is rail(top-left) -> toggle(top-center) -> search(bottom-left, CSS bottom:104px) -> person(top-right, CSS top:14px right:314px) -> route(bottom-left, CSS bottom:168px — visually ABOVE search, yet later in tab order) -> buddies(top-right, CSS top:14px right:18px) -> metrics(bottom bar). A sighted keyboard-only or low-vision user tabbing forward crosses from the top of the screen down to the bottom-left search box, back up to the top-right person panel, back down to a route panel positioned above the search box they just left, back up to the top-right buddy list, and finally down to the bottom metrics bar — reversing vertical direction three times in one pass. Separately, the toast notice (Notice.tsx) is rendered fixed at the visual TOP of the viewport (top:14px, centered) but is the very LAST element in the whole document, so a persistent (non-auto-clearing) error/refusal notice sits at the very end of Tab order despite being the first thing visible on screen.
failure: With a view on screen (no modal, not running), pressing Tab repeatedly from the 'Edit people' button visits: Ring/Force toggle, then the search input (bottom-left) before ever reaching the person-details panel or buddy list positioned at the top of the screen — and, if a persistent worker-error toast is showing, it is reached only after tabbing through every button in the roster rail, layout toggle, search, person panel, route panel, buddy list, and quality panel, even though visually it floats above all of them.
remediation: Reorder the JSX so DOM order follows the panels' visual top-to-bottom, left-to-right layout (rail, toggle, person, buddies, route, search, metrics), or use CSS `order`/flex placement decoupled from DOM order if the visual layout must stay as-is; render Notice near the top of #app's sibling stack (or give it a lower tabindex position) so a persistent notice is reachable early rather than last.
invariant: For any two focusable elements A and B where A is positioned strictly above B on screen (and roughly aligned horizontally, or A is in a left-to-right reading position before B), A should precede B in Tab order — DOM order should not require a keyboard user's focus to move backward (up the screen, after having moved down) more than once per full traversal.

theme: F9 (minimal-disruption recalc / 'preserve current buddies') has no representation anywhere in the app's constraint model, worker protocol, or RosterModal props, and building it would fan out across several files that currently have no notion of a prior
summary: Independently traced (not just re-read) the fan-out F9 requires: ConstraintKind ('required'|'prohibited') would need a third concept for priors, but priors are structurally different from the user-typed rows ConstraintsEditor/NamedPair model (derived from the PREVIOUS view's edges rather than typed by the user), so naively adding a 'prior' variant to ConstraintKind would leak into the manual rule editor's KIND_LABEL/select UI where it doesn't belong. Separately, worker/protocol.ts's GenerateRequest/GenerateOptions carry no priorWeight/priorHard field even though the core (lib/src/core/constraints.ts addPrior/priorHard, index.ts priorWeight) already supports it, and RosterModal — the only 'Edit people' surface — receives only names/settings/rules from App.tsx, never view.edges, so there is no data source in scope to derive priors from at the toggle's natural UI location.
failure: n/a - no caller exists yet; mechanically confirmed via grep -rn 'priorWeight|priorHard|addPrior|ConstraintKind' app/src, which returns only the required/prohibited machinery and zero prior references
remediation: When F9 is scheduled: (1) pass the live view (or at least view.edges + view.names) into RosterModal from App.tsx; (2) add a name-keyed prior-derivation analogous to resolveNamedPairs but sourced from previous edges, not typed rows; (3) extend GenerateOptions with priorWeight/priorHard and thread it through worker/generate.ts's toConstraints call (cons.addPrior/cons.priorHard), kept independent of ConstraintPair/ConstraintKind so it never surfaces in ConstraintsEditor's UI.
invariant: for every exported name in lib/src/core's prior API (addPrior, priorHard, priorWeight, priorsKeptFraction), grep -rn '<name>' app/src returns at least one caller once F9 ships; until then it returns none, which is the mechanical no-caller test this finding is filed against

theme: once a roster is disconnected, the quality score improves as the roster gets worse, so the optimizer breaks it up further and reports better numbers
summary: penalizedAspl applies a flat +10*n penalty to any disconnected graph while ASPL is averaged over reachable pairs only, so splitting a disconnected graph further strictly LOWERS the objective; polishConstrained (and polish) therefore hill-climb into deeper fragmentation, and the ASPL/diameter reported to the caller improve while largestComponentFraction collapses.
failure: buildConstrainedBuddyGraph(16, 2, cons) with cons prohibiting [[1,2],[12,15],[10,13],[12,13],[3,10],[12,14],[11,14],[5,11],[8,13],[7,10],[9,15],[13,15],[5,6],[2,12],[0,9],[2,13],[0,14],[6,10],[9,11],[4,10],[13,14],[8,9]] and DEFAULT options (auto-polish is on at n<=120) returns aspl=1.2777, diameter=3, report.connected=false, report.largestComponentFraction=0.25. The same call with {polish:false} returns aspl=4.9565, diameter=13, largestComponentFraction=0.875. Polish took the roster from one 14-person group to five fragments and the displayed average separation 'improved' from 5.0 to 1.3. Across 200 seeds on that instance every run ended worse than its input (best lcf reached 0.375 vs 0.875 at the start). Sibling on the unconstrained export, which has no connectivity guard at all: g = 12-cycle on 0..11 plus 4-cycle on 12..15; polish(g,{mode:'hill',seed:1,maxIters:4000}) returns 4 components (sizes 5,4,4,3), lcf 0.75 -> 0.3125, and reports aspl 1.36, connected false.
remediation: Make the disconnection penalty monotone in fragmentation instead of flat, so no move that increases the number of components can ever lower the energy — e.g. penalize per stranded vertex / per extra component (aspl + 10*n*(n - largestComponentSize) or + 10*n*(components-1)), and count unreachable ordered pairs at a value above any achievable finite distance rather than dropping them from the mean. Per lib/CLAUDE.md the objective is mirrored, so change reference-python/core.py penalized_aspl (and constrained_gen.py's measure) first, regenerate fixtures, then mirror. Close the whole theme, not the reported call: the identical flat penalty is consumed by polish.ts:39 energy() (which has NO wasConnected guard, only the energy comparison) and by constrainedGreedy.ts:135 constrainedMeasure, and constrainedGreedy.ts:155's guard must be widened from 'was connected and now is not' to 'component count must never increase'.
invariant: For every Graph g, every Constraints c, every seed and iteration budget: connectedComponents(polishConstrained(g,c,opts)).length <= connectedComponents(g).length AND largestComponentFraction(polishConstrained(g,c,opts)) >= largestComponentFraction(g); the same must hold for polish(g,opts).graph in both modes. Equivalently, for any two graphs on the same n, penalizedAspl must be strictly greater for the one with strictly more connected components.

theme: an aggregate computed over reachable pairs only is surfaced as if it described the whole roster, so a split group reads as tighter than a whole one
summary: allPairsSummary.diameter (and aspl) are maxima/means over reachable pairs only and are surfaced verbatim as BuddyResult.diameter / ConstrainedBuddyResult.diameter, so a disconnected roster reports a small finite 'longest separation' — the exact convention eccentricity's own docstring (metrics.ts:97) rejects, where it deliberately returns Infinity instead of a small finite number for the same situation.
failure: For the n=16,k=2 instance above, buildConstrainedBuddyGraph reports diameter: 3 and aspl: 1.2777 for a graph in which most pairs of people cannot reach each other at all; eccentricity(g, v) on the very same graph returns Infinity for every v. The two exported metrics disagree about what 'distance to an unreachable person' means, and the one a UI shows for 'longest separation' is the one that reads as excellent.
remediation: Pick one convention across the module and apply it to the surfaced fields: either return Infinity for diameter (and aspl) when summary.connected is false, matching eccentricity, or rename the fields to state the restriction (asplWithinGroups / diameterWithinGroups) and require the connectivity flag to travel with them. If the Infinity route is taken, change reference-python/core.py all_pairs_summary first and regenerate fixtures, since fixture parity currently pins the finite value.
invariant: For every Graph g and every vertex v: eccentricity(g,v) === Infinity implies that every consumer-facing distance aggregate for g (allPairsSummary(g).diameter and .aspl, BuddyResult.diameter/.aspl, ConstrainedBuddyResult.diameter/.aspl) is also Infinity — i.e. the module never reports a finite 'distance' aggregate for a graph whose connectivity flag is false.

theme: the polish stage's cost gate is an iteration count keyed on n alone, so the default-options cost at the threshold is tens of seconds and is non-monotone in n
summary: resolveWantPolish enables a 20000-iteration polish pass whenever n <= 120, and polish's per-iteration cost is O(n·m + m log m) (a full edgeList() + allPairsSummary() re-measure). The threshold bounds n but nothing bounds the product, so the most expensive input on the entire unconstrained path sits just below the gate. Measured with default options: buildBuddyGraph(120,12) = 33.0 s (reproduced 34.0 s), buildBuddyGraph(120,4) = 18.5 s, buildBuddyGraph(121,12) = 0.1 s, buildBuddyGraph(300,12) = 1.0 s — a 300x cost cliff, and cost that DECREASES with n. This is default configuration, present-day reachable from the app: app/src/worker/generate.ts calls buildBuddyGraph(n,k,options) with polish:'auto', n up to MAX_ROSTER_N=1000 and k up to BUDDY_MAX=12, so a 120-name roster at 12 buddies runs ~33 s per generate and again per seed-bump reroll (in a worker, so the tab is not frozen — but app/src/io/feasibility.ts only warns above n>300, i.e. the slow case is exactly the one that gets no warning). It also contradicts the stated rationale: lib/CLAUDE.md justifies the n<=120 cap as what keeps polish affordable, and docs/findings/FINDINGS.md sizes polish in TIME ('thorough (8 s) polish budget'), while the shipped budget is a bare count that costs 4x that at the cap.
failure: buildBuddyGraph(120, 12) with default options returns after 33.0 s; buildBuddyGraph(121, 12) returns after 0.1 s. Same k, one more person, 300x less work.
remediation: Make the polish budget a work budget, not a count: derive maxIters from a declared cost ceiling (e.g. iters = clamp(BUDGET / (n·m))) and gate auto-polish on that modelled work rather than on `n <= 120` alone, so density/k participate. Pin the invariant with a test asserting default-option modelled work is bounded by the constant AND monotone in n across the old threshold (n=119..122 at k=BUDDY_MAX), which fails today by construction of the cliff. Update lib/CLAUDE.md's 'auto-polish is capped at n<=120' rationale with the measured cost at the cap.
invariant: For all (n, k) accepted by buildBuddyGraph, the modelled polish work under DEFAULT options — iterations × per-iteration cost, i.e. iters·n·m where m is the edge count of the seed graph — is <= one declared constant budget; equivalently, the iteration budget must be derived from that budget rather than fixed, so that default-option generation cost is monotone non-decreasing in n at fixed k (today it is not: cost(120,k) >> cost(121,k)).

theme: the unconstrained generator has no work budget, so an (n,k) the constrained sibling explicitly refuses as unrunnable is accepted and runs for tens of minutes
summary: ringGreedy's only size gate is MAX_CACHED_N (5000), documented in-file as a MEMORY bound on the n×n distance cache ('~100 MB at this n'); the same comment concedes completion is ~O(n³) time and no gate bounds it. k is not bounded at all beyond k>=2. The constrained path treats this exact class as a blocking hazard — MAX_CONSTRAINED_WORK + constrainedWork(n,k) exist solely to refuse dense-k rosters, with a whole findings doc (docs/findings/constrained-generation-cost-and-caps.md) explaining that the n-cap alone is insufficient — but buildBuddyGraph/ringGreedy get neither the work model nor the refusal. Measured: validate(new Constraints(1000), 999) refuses with 'roster size 1000 with 999 buddies each is too large to generate in reasonable time', while buildBuddyGraph(1000, 999, {polish:false}) accepted the identical (n,k) and had not returned after 22 minutes (killed). Same asymmetry at (5000,12): validate refuses; ringGreedy accepts (n <= MAX_CACHED_N). Sparse scaling measured at ~n³: (500,4)=0.55 s, (1000,4)=5.4 s, (1500,4)=16.8 s, (1000,12)=38.5 s, so the largest accepted sparse input (5000,12) extrapolates to tens of minutes. Present-day app reachability is bounded by app-side clamps (n<=1000, k<=12 → 38 s in a worker); the unbounded case is reachable from any direct consumer of the published package, and lib/CLAUDE.md asserts the opposite ('The generators that ARE the untrusted surface are capped (MAX_CACHED_N, MAX_CONSTRAINED_N, MAX_CONSTRAINED_WORK)').
failure: buildBuddyGraph(1000, 999, {polish:false}) does not return within 22 minutes; validate(new Constraints(1000), 999) refuses the same (n,k) in under 1 ms as 'too large to generate in reasonable time'.
remediation: Give ringGreedy a work budget in the same shape as MAX_CONSTRAINED_WORK: a monotone model of its actual cost (~n²·edgesAdded ≈ n³·min(k,n-1)/2, which is worse than constrainedWork) compared against a constant in graph.ts, enforced as a throw in ringGreedy alongside the existing MAX_CACHED_N check and surfaced through buildBuddyGraph's documented throw contract. Ratchet with a property test over integer (n,k) asserting the accept-set containment above, and correct the 'the untrusted generators are capped' claim in lib/CLAUDE.md.
invariant: For all integer n >= 0 and k >= 0, if any generation entry point ACCEPTS (n,k) (does not throw or refuse) then its modelled work is <= that path's declared budget. In particular the accept-sets must not disagree across paths for the same cost class: there is no (n,k) that validate() refuses as 'too large to generate' but ringGreedy/buildBuddyGraph accept (ringGreedy's own model must be at least as strict, since its per-edge cost is O(n²) cache update, not O(n) BFS).

theme: numeric fields of the options object are taken on faith while n and k are validated, so a non-finite budget becomes an unbounded loop
summary: polishConstrained uses `opts.iters ?? 8000` directly as the loop bound (`for (let it = 0; it < iters; it++)`), and polish.ts:48 does the same with `opts.maxIters ?? 20000` (`while (iters < maxIters)`). Neither is checked for finiteness, integrality or sign, unlike every other numeric input in the core (n, k, and even Graph's ctor are guarded). Infinity is directly obtainable from a JSON settings object — JSON has no Infinity literal, but JSON.parse('{"polishIters":1e999}').polishIters === Infinity (verified) — and buildBuddyGraph/buildConstrainedBuddyGraph forward polishIters straight through. Verified: buildConstrainedBuddyGraph(30,4,new Constraints(30),{polish:true,polishIters:Infinity}) and buildBuddyGraph(30,4,{polish:true,polishIters:1e18}) both had to be killed by timeout; the only loop exit is edges.length < 2, so with >= 2 edges neither ever terminates. This also breaks buildConstrainedBuddyGraph's documented 'refuses, never throws' contract in the worst way — it neither refuses nor returns. The same unvalidated-option class produces garbage rather than a hang elsewhere: buildBuddyGraph(20,4,{minSeparation:NaN}) returns finalMinSeparation: NaN (a numeric result field that JSON.stringify writes as null), and minSeparation:-5 returns finalMinSeparation:-5. Not reachable from the app today — app/src/worker/protocol.ts's GenerateOptions carries only minSeparation/polish/seed, and importGraph sanitizes those — hence suggestion, not blocking; it is reachable from any direct consumer of the published package.
failure: buildConstrainedBuddyGraph(30, 4, new Constraints(30), {polish: true, polishIters: Infinity}) never returns (killed at 10 s; the loop bound is literally Infinity). Secondary: buildBuddyGraph(20, 4, {minSeparation: NaN}).finalMinSeparation === NaN.
remediation: Validate the options object where n and k are validated: in buildBuddyGraph/buildConstrainedBuddyGraph and in polish/polishConstrained, coerce or refuse non-integer/non-finite/negative polishIters|maxIters|iters (and minSeparation) instead of using them as loop bounds. Property-test: for every entry point and every options field, a non-finite/non-integer/negative value either throws/refuses or produces the same result as the documented default, and the call completes within a bounded step count.
invariant: For every exported entry point, every loop bound derived from an options object is a finite non-negative integer — a value outside that domain is refused (throw on the unconstrained path / refusal on the constrained path) or replaced by the documented default before use; consequently every call returns in work bounded by a function of (n, k) and that finite budget. Corollary for the same fix: no numeric field of a non-refused result is NaN.

theme: tag compilation materializes O(n²) pair constraints and validates nothing about n, so the size gate can never run
summary: Constraints.fromTags takes n on faith — no Number.isInteger / MAX_ROSTER check, unlike degreeOf (same file, line 39), the Graph ctor, and validate — and then materializes one Set key per same-tag pair. Measured: fromTags(3000, Array(3000).fill('A')) takes 3.4 s and builds 4 498 500 prohibited keys; the cost is paid inside the constructor, so validate()'s MAX_CONSTRAINED_N refusal never gets a chance to run (this is the 'gate after the work it is meant to bound' shape). fromTags(2e7, []) runs a pure 2e7-iteration loop with no allocation and no guard, so a large non-integer-checked n is a straight time sink. Filed as DEFERRAL per the reporting contract: grep shows no caller outside lib/test/constrained.test.ts — the app never calls fromTags — so nothing untrusted reaches it in the current tree. The O(n²) materialization half is already tracked in lib/CLAUDE.md's known limitations ('Sanitize + size-check tags when F6 lands'); the missing n validation is not.
failure: Constraints.fromTags(3000, new Array(3000).fill('A')) spends 3.4 s and 4.5M Set keys before any validate() can refuse; Constraints.fromTags(1e15, []) loops with no guard at all.
remediation: Reuse the same n guard degreeOf already has, and pre-count group sizes (one O(n) pass over tags) to compute sum(size·(size-1)/2) and refuse against a declared pair cap before the double loop. Defer until a caller exists; keep it in the known-limitations list until then.
invariant: Constraints.fromTags refuses an n that is not an integer in [0, MAX_ROSTER] BEFORE any loop, and refuses a tag distribution whose implied pair count exceeds a declared cap BEFORE materializing pairs — i.e. the number of Set insertions performed by fromTags is bounded by a constant for every (n, tags) it does not refuse.

theme: two functions that document themselves as mirroring each other's precondition checks actually check in a different order, so they can report a different *first* reason for the same invalid input
summary: validateDetailed() (constraints.ts) checks structural validity (out-of-range constraint ids / self-pairs) BEFORE the size/work-budget checks and returns early on a structural hit. checkWellFormed() (constrainedGreedy.ts, the throw-based precondition for direct callers of constrainedGreedy) checks n/MAX_CONSTRAINED_N/k/MAX_CONSTRAINED_WORK FIRST and only calls checkConstraintIds() (the structural mirror) afterward. The comment on checkConstraintIds says it is a 'Throw-on-first mirror of constraints.ts structuralReasons... keep the two checks in step' -- true for the id-validity logic in isolation, but the two entry points disagree on which class of problem is reported first when an input is both oversized AND structurally invalid.
failure: n = 10000 (over MAX_CONSTRAINED_N = 5000) with a constraint pair referencing person 99999: validateDetailed(cons, k) returns [{code:'unknown-person', person:99999, n:10000}] (structural short-circuit fires before the n>MAX_CONSTRAINED_N check ever runs), while a direct call to constrainedGreedy(10000, k, cons) throws "roster size 10000 exceeds the constrained maximum of 5000" (checkWellFormed's n-cap check fires before checkConstraintIds runs). Same malformed input, two different 'first' diagnoses depending on which of the two documented-as-mirrored guards is asked.
remediation: Reorder checkWellFormed to run checkConstraintIds before the size/k/work checks (matching validateDetailed's actual order), or state explicitly in both comments that only the *content* of the structural check is mirrored, not its priority relative to the size/work gates, so a future reader doesn't rely on 'in step' meaning identical precedence.
invariant: for any (n, k, cons) that is both structurally invalid (out-of-range id or self-pair) and over a size/work cap, the Reason.code that would be first in validateDetailed(cons,k) matches the class of error thrown first by calling constrainedGreedy(n,k,cons) directly.

theme: ambiguous constant relationship comment could mislead on whether values are identical
summary: Comment claims UNVISITED is 'distinct from' UNREACHABLE but both are -1
failure: Line 7 defines UNREACHABLE = -1; line 210 defines UNVISITED = -1 with comment 'distinct from bfsDistances' UNREACHABLE'. A maintainer reading 'distinct from' may assume they should have different values, then refactor them apart, breaking the logic. Both serve as visit-markers (same semantic function, different scopes) and sharing -1 is intentional and correct.
remediation: Change the comment from 'distinct from bfsDistances' UNREACHABLE' to 'local redefinition of UNREACHABLE; same value (-1) but function-scoped', or 'per-source BFS marker; mirrors UNREACHABLE sentinel value'.
invariant: When two constants in the same module share an identical value for valid semantic reasons, the comment must clarify the value reuse is intentional, not accidental. The word 'distinct' must not be used to describe a relationship where values are identical.

theme: mixing original and promoted constraint references within same control flow breaks readability
summary: Line 273 checks cons.priorCount; rest of buildConstrainedBuddyGraph (lines 259-282) consistently uses active
failure: Function creates active = withHardPriors(cons) at line 259, then validates active (260), passes active to constrainedGreedy (263) and polishConstrained (276). While functionally equivalent (active and cons have identical priors when priorHard is false), it breaks the local convention. remediation: Change line 273 from 'cons.priorCount > 0' to 'active.priorCount > 0' for consistency with lines 260, 263, 271, 276.
invariant: Within a single function where a promoted variant (active) is derived from an original (cons), references to the constraint set should use active consistently unless the comment explicitly justifies using the original.

theme: an attacker-supplied field in the options object turns the polish stage into unbounded work — the MAX_POLISH_WORK budget is advisory, not authoritative
summary: `resolveWantPolish` honours an explicit `polish: true` without ever consulting `MAX_POLISH_WORK`, so the single most expensive input on the default path — the exact 33 s case the constant was introduced to kill — is still reachable by setting one boolean.

theme: an attacker-supplied field in the options object turns the polish stage into unbounded work — the MAX_POLISH_WORK budget is advisory, not authoritative
summary: `checkedIterations` validates the TYPE of `polishIters` (integer, non-negative, finite) but never its MAGNITUDE, so any large finite integer passes the guard verbatim and becomes the polish loop bound — the sibling one boundary over from the Infinity case the guard was written for.
failure: `JSON.parse('{"polishIters":1e15}').polishIters` is 1e15, for which `Number.isInteger` is true and `< 0` is false, so `checkedIterations` returns it unchanged and it lands in `polish(g, { maxIters: 1e15 })`. That single change subsumes the existing type checks (Infinity/NaN/negative all fail the same comparison) and closes both this and the `polish: true` sibling with one rule, so the polish stage has one ceiling rather than a type guard plus a bypassable flag. Replace the [Infinity, NaN, -1, 1.5, -Infinity] case table with the invariant below.
invariant: For every (n, k, options), the number of polish iterations actually executed satisfies `polishWork(n, k, iters) <= MAX_POLISH_WORK` — for ALL values of `options.polishIters` and `options.polish`, not an enumerated set of malformed ones.

theme: a size gate that runs after the work it is meant to bound — Constraints.fromTags builds O(n^2) pair keys inside the constructor, before validate can refuse anything
summary: `Constraints.fromTags` takes `n` entirely on faith — unlike `degreeOf` in the same file, the `Graph` constructor and `validate`, all of which guard it — and then runs an unguarded `for (i < n) { for (j < n) }` materializing one Set key per same-tag pair, so the cost is paid before any cap can be consulted.
failure: `fromTags(1e15, [])` enters `for (let i = 0; i < 1e15; i++)` with no guard whatsoever and never returns; `fromTags(3000, Array(3000).fill('A'))` spends ~3.4 s building 4.5M keys and at tens of millions of pairs the Set construction throws before `validate`'s MAX_CONSTRAINED_N refusal is ever reached. Also `NaN` as a tag value never equals itself, so `prohibit_same` silently produces no constraints for that group. Filed as a deferral, not gating: `grep` finds no caller of `fromTags` outside `lib/test` — the tag UI is P2 and explicitly deferred in app/CLAUDE.md — so nothing untrusted reaches it in the current tree, and this is already recorded in lib/CLAUDE.md's known-limitations list. Repeating it here only so the log is complete for this round.
remediation: When the tag UI lands (not before): validate `n` against MAX_ROSTER/MAX_CONSTRAINED_N as the first statement, then pre-count group sizes in one O(n) pass and refuse against a pair cap (sum of C(size,2)) BEFORE the double loop runs, and reject non-finite/NaN tag values by normalizing them to null.
invariant: `Constraints.fromTags(n, tags, policy)` returns or throws in time O(n + emitted pairs) with emitted pairs <= a stated cap, for all n and all tags — it never performs work proportional to an unvalidated n.

theme: the polish work budget is documented and tested as authoritative, but a fixed 100-evaluation calibration phase runs outside it, so the real cost exceeds MAX_POLISH_WORK by an unbounded factor exactly where the clamp bites hardest
summary: `polish`'s anneal temperature calibration performs up to 100 full O(n·m) all-pairs measurements before the main loop, and `boundedIterations`/MAX_POLISH_WORK bound only the main loop — so the clamp that is supposed to make the budget authoritative is silently bypassed.
failure: Reproduced. `polish(g, {mode:"anneal", maxIters: 0})` on a 300-vertex 4-regular graph takes 587 ms while `mode:"hill", maxIters: 0` takes 11 ms — 100 unbudgeted energy evaluations. End-to-end on the reachable public path: for (n=400, k=100) — allowed by MAX_GREEDY_WORK (3.2e9 <= 1e10) — `boundedIterations` clamps to floor(MAX_POLISH_WORK / polishWork(400,100,1)) = 72 iterations, i.e. a budgeted 5.76e8 work units. Measured on that graph: hill(72) = 4817 ms, anneal(72) = 10822 ms, calibration-only = 6154 ms. `buildBuddyGraph` always uses mode "anneal", so `buildBuddyGraph(400, 100, {polish: true})` actually spends ~1.38e9 work units — 2.4x the budget the comment on MAX_POLISH_WORK and the test block "MAX_POLISH_WORK cannot be stepped around" both assert is authoritative. The overshoot ratio is 100/clamp and grows without bound as n·m grows; the existing tests only exercise (120,12) where clamp=6666 and the 100 extra evals are 1.5% — invisible. This is exactly the hole the existing suite was written to close, one code line to the left of where it looked.

theme: a headline number reported to the organizer describes a graph that is not the graph that was returned — polish rewires after the number is computed and nothing re-derives it
summary: `BuddyResult.finalMinSeparation` is `ringGreedy`'s pre-polish target and is never re-derived after the polish pass, which is not separation-aware — so the returned graph routinely contains buddy pairs closer than the separation the result advertises.
failure: Reproduced. `buildBuddyGraph(16, 5)` returns `finalMinSeparation: 3, polished: true, girth: 3`. Tracing the two stages: `ringGreedy(16, 5, {mind: 5, repair: true})` returns `finalMind = 3` and a graph with `girth = 4` — consistent, since linking two people 3 apart closes a 4-cycle. The polish pass then swaps edges with no separation term in its objective and drops girth to 3, i.e. some pair became buddies while only 2 degrees apart. The result still reports `finalMinSeparation: 3`. Same failure at (20,5), (24,5), (30,5), (20,6), (24,6) — every one reports 3 while delivering girth 3. An organizer told "minimum separation 3" is handed a triangle. No test asserts any relation between `finalMinSeparation` and the delivered graph; `identity.test.ts:33` only pins `finalMind` against the pre-polish fixture, so the whole suite passes.
remediation: Either derive the reported value from the returned graph (`girth(g) - 1`, clamped, computed after polish — `girth` is already computed there) or rename/redocument the field as the generator's target rather than an achieved property and stop returning it as a quality metric. Sibling to name before closing: `GreedyResult.finalMind`'s own doc comment claims "the mind target actually achieved", which is only true of `ringGreedy`'s own output; whichever way this is resolved, that claim has to move too.
invariant: For every (n, k, options), the BuddyResult r returned by buildBuddyGraph satisfies `r.finalMinSeparation <= girth(graphOf(r.edges)) - 1` whenever that girth is finite — the advertised minimum separation never exceeds the minimum separation actually present in the returned edge set.

theme: a bound advertised as a floor on what is achievable reports a value no graph can meet, so 'provably optimal' scoring against it is wrong
summary: The `shell === 0` padding branch in `mooreLowerBounds` advances `diameterLb` to `dist` even when `remaining` is already 0, producing a diameter lower bound strictly greater than the diameter of the graph that meets the ASPL bound.
failure: Reproduced. `mooreLowerBounds(2, 1)` returns `{ asplLb: 1, diameterLb: 2 }`. K2 — the unique 1-regular graph on 2 vertices, which `buildConstrainedBuddyGraph(2, 1, new Constraints(2))` actually builds — has ASPL 1 and diameter 1. The bound claims no such graph can have diameter below 2. Trace: after the first shell, `remaining = 0` and `diameterLb = 1`; `dist` is then incremented to 2 and, because `k === 1` sets `shell = 0`, the padding block runs unconditionally and overwrites `diameterLb = 2` while adding `dist * 0 = 0` to `total` — so the ASPL bound stays correct and only the diameter bound is corrupted. Swept n in [2,60] x k in [1,60]: (2,1) is the sole violation. The same defect exists in `reference-python/core.py` `moore_lower_bounds` (lines 259-264), so oracle parity does not catch it and `identity.test.ts:50` pins the wrong value if a k=1 fixture is ever added; `metrics.test.ts` only checks (10,3).
remediation: Guard the padding block on `remaining > 0` (`if (shell === 0 && remaining > 0)`) in both `bounds.ts` and `reference-python/core.py` — change the Python first and regenerate fixtures, per the mirror rule. `total` is unaffected either way, so no ASPL fixture moves.
invariant: For all integers n > 1 and k > 0, `mooreLowerBounds(n,k).diameterLb <= mooreLowerBounds(n,k).asplLb * (n-1)` — the farthest shell the bound charges for cannot lie beyond the total distance it accumulated.

theme: the result reports no signal that the requested buddy count could not be delivered, and the headline quality score silently mixes wiring quality with that degree shortfall
summary: `asplGap` is scored against the Moore bound for the REQUESTED k while the generator's demotion floor can deliver a strictly smaller uniform degree, so a graph that is provably optimal for what it delivered reports a large gap, and `regular: true` reads as "everyone got k buddies" when they did not.
failure: Reproduced. `buildBuddyGraph(8, 6)` returns `degreeMin: 3, degreeMax: 3, regular: true, aspl: 1.571, asplGap: 0.375`. The delivered graph is 3-regular, not 6-regular: `mooreLowerBounds(8,3).asplLb` is 11/7 = 1.571, so the graph is exactly optimal for its delivered degree, yet the result advertises "37.5% off optimal". Cause: `ringGreedy`'s demotion stops at `curMind > 3`, so once the graph reaches diameter 2 no pair is >= 3 apart and both `findPair` and `repairDegrees` (minDist 3) stop, leaving degrees far below k. Same shape at (8,4) -> 3-regular gap 0.100, (8,5) -> 3-regular gap 0.222, (12,5) -> 4-regular gap 0.059, (12,6) -> 4-regular gap 0.125. This is oracle-consistent (the demotion floor mirrors reference-python), so it is a reporting defect rather than an algorithm divergence — but nothing in BuddyResult states that k was not met beyond the reader noticing degreeMax < k, and `regular: true` actively points the other way. lib/CLAUDE.md documents only the `k >= n` cap, not this k < n shortfall.
remediation: Report the shortfall explicitly rather than folding it into the gap: either score `asplGap` against `mooreLowerBounds(n, degreeMax)` so 0 means "optimal for what was delivered", or add a field carrying the requested-vs-delivered degree so a consumer can distinguish "badly wired" from "could not reach k buddies". Do not close this by only documenting `regular` — the sibling is `asplGap`, and vice versa.
invariant: For every (n, k), the BuddyResult r from buildBuddyGraph satisfies `r.asplGap === asplGap(r.aspl, n, r.degreeMax)` — the gap is scored against the degree actually delivered, so any graph meeting the Moore bound for its own delivered degree reports exactly 0.

theme: a caller-supplied iteration count becomes main-thread work that the work budget claims to bound but does not, because the cost model has no per-iteration constant
summary: `boundedIterations` clamps polish to `floor(MAX_POLISH_WORK / polishWork(n,k,1))`, and `polishWork` models per-iteration cost as `iters*n*m` with no constant term. Real per-iteration cost has a large fixed floor (edgeList build + sort, `new Set` in proposeSwap, one Int32Array per BFS source, `g.copy()`), so as n*m shrinks the afforded iteration count explodes: at (n=3,k=2) the model affords 64,000,000 iterations. The doc comment on this function asserts the budget is "authoritative rather than advisory" and that "ANY value is clamped to what MAX_POLISH_WORK affords" — that is true of the model and false of the wall clock. The existing budget tests in optimizer.props.test.ts pin only (120,12) and (30,4), where the clamp binds to a few thousand iterations, so the regime where the model inverts is untested — the case-table failure mode this review contract warns about.
failure: MEASURED: `buildBuddyGraph(3, 2, { polishIters: 1e9 })` -> 35,714 ms (no `polish: true` needed; auto-polish is already on at this size, and 1e9 survives the Number.isInteger/>=0 check). `buildBuddyGraph(4, 2, { polish: true, polishIters: 1e9 })` -> 33,532 ms. `buildConstrainedBuddyGraph(4, 2, new Constraints(4), { polishIters: 1e9 })` -> 37,937 ms, i.e. the documented "refuses, never throws" entry point neither refuses nor returns for 38 s. `polishIters: 1e308` at (10,3) -> 16,671 ms. Control with default options: 12 ms. In a browser this is a ~36 s frozen tab for a THREE-PERSON roster, driven by one integer in a settings object. Present-day reachability: the lib's own public API (this is the reviewed component); the BuddyGraph app never passes polishIters today, so app reachability is nil — this is a defect in the guard, not a live app exploit.
remediation: Give the clamp a positive per-iteration floor and an absolute ceiling: in `boundedIterations`, use `Math.min(requested, Math.floor(MAX_POLISH_WORK / (POLISH_ITER_OVERHEAD + perIteration)), MAX_POLISH_ITERS)` with `POLISH_ITER_OVERHEAD` calibrated to the measured fixed cost of one polish iteration (edge-list build + proposal + copy). Keep `polishWork` itself unchanged for the auto-polish GATE, since polishWork(120,4)/polishWork(121,4) is what the fixtures and the reroll boundary test pin — only the iteration clamp needs the floor. Ratchet the invariant into optimizer.props.test.ts as a property over arbitrary (n,k,v) on the resolved iteration count, not as more (n,k) cases.
invariant: For all n, k and all `polishIters` values v, the number of polish iterations actually executed, I(v,n,k), satisfies I(v,n,k) * (C + polishWork(n,k,1)) <= MAX_POLISH_WORK for a fixed constant C > 0 — equivalently, sup over all n,k,v of I(v,n,k) is a finite constant independent of n and k. Today I is unbounded as n*m -> 0 (I = 64,000,000 at n=3,k=2 versus 1,209 at n=120,k=12).

theme: a caller-supplied iteration count becomes main-thread work that the work budget claims to bound but does not, because the guard sits in the wrapper instead of at the loop
summary: `polish` (polish.ts) and `polishConstrained` (constrainedGreedy.ts) are both exported from the package index as public API with documented `maxIters` / `iters` options, and both use that value directly as the sole loop bound (`while (iters < maxIters)` / `for (let it = 0; it < iters; it++)`) with no type or magnitude validation. The only other exit is "fewer than two edges". `boundedIterations` in index.ts was added specifically because `JSON.parse('{"polishIters":1e999}')` yields Infinity — but it guards only the two builder wrappers, leaving the primitives that actually contain the loop exported and unguarded. The guard is one call frame away from the loop it is meant to bound.
failure: MEASURED: `polish(ring(20), { maxIters: JSON.parse('{"maxIters":1e999}').maxIters })` never returns — killed by an external 60 s timeout, and the blocked event loop prevented even an unref'd 15 s watchdog timer from firing, so it is a hard main-thread hang rather than a slow return. `polishConstrained(g, cons, { iters: Infinity })` has the identical shape (`opts.iters ?? 8000`, no validation) and the same single loop exit. polish.ts carries no "low-level primitive, call validate first" disclaimer at all, unlike constrainedGreedy.ts.

The wrappers then become redundant rather than load-bearing, which is the correct direction for a guard.
invariant: For every function exported from lib/src/core/index.ts that accepts an iteration count, the number of loop iterations executed is finite for all inputs and bounded by a constant derived from MAX_POLISH_WORK — i.e. no exported loop uses a caller-supplied number as its only bound without first clamping it. Checkable by calling every such export with Infinity / NaN / 1e308 / 1e15 under a wall-clock assertion.

theme: a quadratic materialization runs upstream of every size gate, so the gate that would refuse the roster never gets to run
summary: `Constraints.fromTags` validates no `n` at all (unlike `degreeOf` in the same file, the `Graph` constructor, and `validate`) and runs a full O(n^2) double loop materializing one Set key per same-tag pair. Every size gate in the system — MAX_CONSTRAINED_N, MAX_CONSTRAINED_WORK, MAX_ROSTER — lives in `validate`/`checkWellFormed`, strictly downstream. Filed as deferral per the no-live-caller rule: `fromTags` has no caller outside lib/test, and lib/CLAUDE.md already records it as deliberately deferred until the tag UI lands. Reported here with numbers because I reproduced it and the measurement is sharper than the recorded one (the recorded note says 3.4 s at n=3000; the throw case is worse).
failure: MEASURED: `Constraints.fromTags(200000, new Array(200000).fill('household'))` spends 24,746 ms and then throws a native `RangeError: Set maximum size exceeded` — for a roster `validate` would have refused instantly (200000 > MAX_CONSTRAINED_N = 5000). The failure is a raw RangeError from a constructor, not a refusal, so a caller following the documented "call validate() first" discipline still cannot avoid it. Even at a LEGAL roster size the amplification bites: `fromTags(5000, Array(5000).fill('h'))` = 21,199 ms building 12,497,500 keys, and the subsequent `validate(c, 4)` — which the work model accepts, since constrainedWork(5000,4) = 1e8 exactly equals MAX_CONSTRAINED_WORK — takes a further 28,020 ms, because prohibitedPairs() re-materializes all 12.5M tuples on each of its three call sites. ~49 s total from a 5000-entry tag column.
remediation: Guard `n` at the top of `fromTags` (integer, 0..MAX_CONSTRAINED_N) and pre-count group sizes with a single O(n) pass, refusing against an explicit pair cap (sum over groups of size*(size-1)/2 <= MAX_PROHIBITED_PAIRS) BEFORE the double loop — so the cost is refused rather than paid. Separately, cache `prohibitedPairs()` or iterate the key Set directly in validateDetailed instead of rebuilding tuple arrays three times.
invariant: For all n, tags and policy, `Constraints.fromTags` either throws a domain error before adding any key, or returns having added at most MAX_PROHIBITED_PAIRS keys; and its total work is O(n + returned pair count). No input causes it to exceed that pair cap or to raise a native RangeError.
