theme: return value allows silent misuse when input is refused
summary: buildConstrainedBuddyGraph returns empty but type-valid structures (buddies=[[],[],[]], edges=[]) when refused, making it easy to forget checking report.refusals
failure: ConstrainedBuddyResult has non-nullable buddies/edges arrays. When refused, refusedResult returns {buddies: Array(size).fill([]), edges: [], ...}. A caller can iterate these fields without error even when the input was refused: 'for (const b of result.buddies) { }' works silently on empty arrays. The documentation (line 241) warns 'read report.refusals first' but the TypeScript type system does not enforce it—any field access is valid and silent.
remediation: Consider using a discriminated union return type: ConstrainedBuddyResult = SuccessResult | RefusedResult, where RefusedResult has only report and no buddies/edges. This would make the TypeScript compiler catch accidental field access. Alternatively, use a sealed pattern: if (result.report.refusals.length > 0) { return /* handle refusal */ } enforced by a linter rule.
invariant: When a builder function can refuse input, its return type should make the failure path structurally distinct from the success path, or use a runtime guard documented in the type

theme: the Graph container's own mutators do not enforce its structural invariants, so a bad vertex index half-applies an edge and leaves a silently corrupt graph instead of refusing
summary: Graph.addEdge writes adj[u] before touching adj[v], so an out-of-range v throws only after the first half of the edge has been added. A caller that catches the error keeps a Graph whose adjacency is asymmetric and contains a non-vertex, and whose own accessors then disagree with each other. The class docstring claims the symmetry invariant 'can only be mutated through addEdge/removeEdge', yet addEdge is the single mutator with no argument check — while the constructor guards n, constraints.degreeOf guards n, and metrics.checkVertex guards caller-supplied indices for shortestPath/eccentricity for exactly this reason. Same root, second symptom: exported bfsDistances takes an unchecked source and throws a raw TypeError ('Cannot read properties of undefined') where its two siblings refuse with a clear message. No current in-repo caller is unvalidated (app/src/io/importGraph.ts range-checks every edge; app/src/state/useGraph.ts and app/src/worker/generate.ts consume lib output), which is why this is a suggestion rather than blocking.
failure: const g = new Graph(3); g.addEdge(0,1); try { g.addEdge(0,5); } catch {}  ->  g.adj[0] is Set{1,5} (5 is not a vertex); g.degrees() === [2,1,0] (degree sum 3, odd, violating the handshake invariant the numEdges() floor comment relies on); g.numEdges() === 1 while g.edgeList().length === 2 and edgeList() returns [0,5]; g.copy() reproduces the asymmetry without error. Separately, bfsDistances(new Graph(3), 5) throws TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'adj[u]' iteration), whereas shortestPath/eccentricity on the same index throw 'source 5 must be an integer in [0, 2]'.
remediation: Validate both endpoints at the top of addEdge (Number.isInteger and 0 <= x < this.n) and throw BEFORE any mutation, mirroring the constructor's message style; apply the same guard to removeEdge and hasEdge so the read path cannot report a phantom edge either. Route bfsDistances' source through the existing metrics.checkVertex so all three BFS entry points refuse a bad index identically. Ratchet the invariant into test/paths.props.test.ts or a new graph.props.test.ts as a property over arbitrary call sequences that include throwing calls.
invariant: For any Graph reachable through the public API — after ANY sequence of constructor/addEdge/removeEdge calls, including calls that threw — for every u in [0, n) and every v in adj[u]: Number.isInteger(v) && 0 <= v < n && adj[v].has(u); and numEdges() === edgeList().length.

theme: the polish work budget is computed from a per-iteration cost model that omits the dominant term of the work it is meant to bound, so the single enforcement point grants hundreds of times the budget on a large sparse graph
summary: `boundedPolishIterations` models one polish iteration as `POLISH_ITER_OVERHEAD + n*m`, but the iteration's actual cost is `allPairsSummary`, which is Theta(n*(n+m)) — it allocates and fills an Int32Array(n) and runs an n-wide accumulation loop per source regardless of m — so for m << n the divisor is too small by a factor of n/m and the full 20000-iteration grant is handed out.
failure: Reproduced. `const g = new Graph(3000); g.addEdge(0,1); g.addEdge(2,3); g.addEdge(4,5); g.addEdge(6,7); polish(g, { mode: "hill" })` — `boundedPolishIterations(3000, 4, undefined, 20000)` returns the full 20000, and 2000 of those iterations took 67.6 s, i.e. the default call runs ~11 minutes. Measured grants vs true cost: n=1000,m=4 -> 20000 iters, modelled 8.1e7 but true 2.0e10 (35x over MAX_POLISH_WORK); n=4000,m=4 -> 20000 iters, true 3.2e11 (555x); n=100000,m=4 -> 1442 iters, true 1.4e13 (24980x); n=1000000,m=4 (still inside MAX_ROSTER) -> 144 iters, true 1.4e14 (249447x). `polishConstrained` is the same defect via the same helper: n=2000,m=4 grants the full default 8000 iterations, extrapolating to ~148 s. This is the exact sibling of the already-fixed small-n case that `POLISH_ITER_OVERHEAD` closed — that one was n small and m small; this one is n LARGE and m small, one axis over, and `optimizer.props.test.ts`'s "bounds the exported primitives, not just the wrappers around them" is the contract it breaks. The same omission is present in the gate `polishWork` (graph.ts:172-175): `polishWork(n, 0, iters)` = `iters*64` for any n, so the k=0 auto-polish gate opens at every roster size, and the live-caller instance `buildConstrainedBuddyGraph(5000, 1, cons, { polish: true })` spends 3.2 s of measured polish against a grant the model priced at 46 iterations (mild, but the same undercount).
remediation: Make the divisor the real asymptotic cost by subtraction, not by adding a second cap: in `boundedPolishIterations` use `POLISH_ITER_OVERHEAD + n * (n + m)`, and in `polishWork` use `iters * (POLISH_ITER_OVERHEAD + n * (n + m))` with the same estimated m. `MAX_POLISH_WORK` must be re-derived to 865_280_000 to keep the pinned boundary byte-identical — I checked the arithmetic: new polishWork(120,4,20000) = 865_280_000 (admitted exactly), new polishWork(121,4,20000) = 879_740_000 (refused), new polishWork(120,12,20000) = 2.017e9 (still refused), and the `afforded >= 20000` assertion at (30,4)/(60,4)/(120,4) still holds. After the fix n=4000,m=4 is granted 54 iterations (~4 s) instead of 20000 (~27 min). Note that `n*(n+m)` also fixes the k=0 gate hole, since the n² term no longer vanishes with m.
invariant: For every integer n in [0, MAX_ROSTER] and every m in [0, n*(n-1)/2], and for every `requested`/`fallback`, the granted iteration count times the TRUE per-iteration cost stays inside the budget: `boundedPolishIterations(n, m, requested, fallback) * (POLISH_ITER_OVERHEAD + n * (n + m)) <= MAX_POLISH_WORK + (POLISH_ITER_OVERHEAD + n * (n + m))` (one iteration of slack for the floor). Equivalently and more durably: the divisor the bound uses must be >= the asymptotic cost of one iteration, which is the cost of `allPairsSummary`, Theta(n*(n+m)) — so any future re-model of the objective is held to the same property rather than to these n/m pairs.

theme: numeric options arriving from an untrusted settings object are validated on some entry points and taken on faith on others, so a non-finite value silently turns a stage into a no-op while the result still reports that the stage ran
summary: `polishConstrained` accepts `priorWeight` with no finiteness check (`opts.priorWeight ?? 0`), unlike its sibling `iters`, which `boundedPolishIterations` falls back to a default on. A NaN weight poisons `constrainedMeasure`'s energy, so `next.energy < current - 1e-12` is false for every candidate, every swap is reverted, and the pass returns its input unchanged while `buildConstrainedBuddyGraph` still reports `polished: true`.
failure: Ran it: `const c = new Constraints(20); c.addPrior(0,1); buildConstrainedBuddyGraph(20, 4, c, { priorWeight: NaN })` returns `polished: true` with edges byte-identical to the unpolished graph — the optimizer did 8000 iterations of full O(n·m) re-measurement and accepted nothing. NaN is reachable from a settings object without a NaN literal (`JSON.parse('{"priorWeight":null}').priorWeight` is null, but any arithmetic-derived weight, or `Number(x)` on a non-numeric field, yields NaN). Filed as a deferral by the mechanical rule: `priorWeight`, `addPrior` and `priorHard` have no reference anywhere outside `lib/src/core` and `lib/test` (grep over `app/src` is empty), so nothing untrusted reaches it in the current tree — the priors feature itself is deferred to F9/M4.
remediation: Give `priorWeight` the same treatment `iters` already gets: `const priorWeight = Number.isFinite(opts.priorWeight) ? (opts.priorWeight as number) : 0;` in `polishConstrained`, and the same on `ConstrainedBuddyOptions.priorWeight` in `index.ts`. Closing the theme rather than the case means auditing every numeric option on a public entry point for the same fall-back-to-default discipline (`seed` is already safe via `>>>0`; `minSeparation` is already clamped by `Math.min(..., floor(n/2))`).
invariant: For every public entry point and every numeric option, a non-finite value produces exactly the result the documented default produces: for all non-finite w, `buildConstrainedBuddyGraph(n, k, cons, { priorWeight: w })` returns the same `edges` as `buildConstrainedBuddyGraph(n, k, cons, {})`, and no non-finite option value ever reaches an energy comparison (equivalently: `measure(g).energy` is finite for every reachable graph whenever `penalizedAspl` is finite).

theme: graph.ts's own doc comment justifies hosting every generation pipeline's cost-budget logic there by appeal to avoiding an import cycle, but tracing the actual type signatures shows only one of those exports needs that co-location — the file has organically become the home for three unrelated subsystems' tuning constants rather than the Graph data structure's own concern
summary: graph.ts (line 11-15 doc comment) exports the Graph class plus MAX_ROSTER, MAX_CONSTRAINED_N, MAX_CONSTRAINED_WORK, constrainedWork, MAX_GREEDY_WORK, greedyWork, MAX_POLISH_WORK, POLISH_ITER_OVERHEAD, MAX_POLISH_ITERS, boundedPolishIterations, polishWork and DEFAULT_MIN_SEPARATION — cost-model constants and estimators for the constrained-greedy path, the unconstrained ringGreedy path, and both polish passes, none of which are used by the Graph class itself.
failure: Only `MAX_ROSTER` is actually referenced inside graph.ts (Graph's own constructor guard, line 189). Every other budget export — constrainedWork(n,k), greedyWork(n,k), polishWork(n,k,iters), boundedPolishIterations(n,m,requested,fallback) — takes only plain numbers and never references the Graph type, so none of them has a type-level reason to live in the same file as Graph. They could sit in a standalone zero-import module (call it budgets.ts, alongside the file already named bounds.ts for a different purpose — Moore lower bounds) that graph.ts, constraints.ts, greedy.ts, polish.ts and constrainedGreedy.ts would all import from instead, with graph.ts itself importing only MAX_ROSTER from it for its own constructor check. The stated justification ('this module is also home to the cross-cutting roster/work bounds... so every module can import them without an import cycle') is true of the effect (no cycle exists today) but not the cause (co-location with Graph specifically is not what prevents the cycle — any dependency-free module would do, and one already exists in this same directory under a name, `bounds.ts`, that a reader would reasonably expect to hold exactly this).
remediation: Extract the non-Graph-typed budget constants and estimators (MAX_CONSTRAINED_N/WORK, constrainedWork, MAX_GREEDY_WORK, greedyWork, MAX_POLISH_WORK, POLISH_ITER_OVERHEAD, MAX_POLISH_ITERS, boundedPolishIterations, polishWork, DEFAULT_MIN_SEPARATION) into their own zero-import module; leave MAX_ROSTER and the Graph class in graph.ts, with graph.ts importing MAX_ROSTER back if that split is preferred. This is a mechanical move, not a behavior change, and shrinks graph.ts to what its name and its docstring's first sentence claim it is.
invariant: For every binding exported from graph.ts other than {Graph, ring, MAX_ROSTER}, its parameter and return types contain no reference to Graph — true for every current export, meaning none of them requires co-location with the Graph class for type reasons, only for the file-organization reason the comment gives (which a standalone module would satisfy equally well).

theme: Comment describes budget constraint inaccurately, potentially misleading about how iteration budget is shared between calibration and main loop
summary: Comment says calibration is 'charged against the same budget as the loop', but code runs calibration and main loop independently—each bounded by maxIters, not sharing
failure: A contributor reading the comment might misunderstand the budget model. With maxIters=20000 and edges.length≥100: trials=min(100,edges.length,20000)=100, then main loop runs 20000 iterations independently, for total of 20100 iterations. The 'same budget' phrasing suggests they share (total would be 20000), but they run independently with each capped by maxIters.
remediation: Clarify the comment to say the calibration is now 'bounded by the budget' rather than 'charged against the same budget'. Replace line 70 with: '// Bounded by the iteration budget. These are full O(n·m) energy' and adjust the phrasing to clarify that both calibration and main loop are independently constrained by maxIters, not sharing it.
invariant: The calibration iteration count trials must satisfy: trials ≤ min(100, edges.length, maxIters). If maxIters=0, trials must be 0 (preventing the old 587ms unconditional-calibration issue). The main loop must run exactly maxIters times. A comment claiming they 'share' a budget is false if total work = trials + maxIters can exceed maxIters.

theme: the polish objective lets a soft preference buy a structurally more broken roster, and the guard that is supposed to stop it is weaker than the property the repo claims
summary: polishConstrained's fragmentation guard only compares COMPONENT COUNT, so a swap that simultaneously splits the largest group and merges two small ones passes it — the largest group shrinks while the count is unchanged, at the library's own DEFAULT_PRIOR_WEIGHT of 2.
failure: polishConstrained(g, cons, { seed: 45, iters: 500, priorWeight: 2 }) with n=11, g.edgeList()=[[0,2],[1,4],[1,6],[2,4],[3,8]] and cons priors [[4,10],[3,4],[0,1]] returns a graph whose largestComponentFraction fell from 5/11 (0.4545) to 4/11 (0.3636) with the component count identical at 6 -> 6. A 3000-instance sweep found 7 such cases, several at priorWeight 2 (the value index.ts injects by default whenever priors exist) and priorWeight 5. The arithmetic is why: charging one newly-unreachable pair costs ~ (n - d) / (n(n-1)) < 1 at these sizes, while gaining one prior is worth `priorWeight`, so the prior term added on top of penalizedAspl outweighs it. I could NOT reproduce it through buildConstrainedBuddyGraph in ~1500 targeted scenarios, so the defect is confirmed at the exported primitive, not (yet) at the builder. The existing suite cannot catch it: optimizer.props.test.ts holds `polish` to `largestComponentFraction(out) >= largestComponentFraction(g)` (line 122) but holds polishConstrained only to `components(out) <= components(g)` (line 160) — the sibling property was never carried across.
remediation: Hold polishConstrained to the same property its unconstrained sibling already satisfies: reject any swap whose result has a smaller largest component than the pass started with (compare largest-component size alongside, or instead of, the component count — connectedComponents is already being computed in constrainedMeasure, so the size is free). Then add the largestComponentFraction assertion to the polishConstrained block of optimizer.props.test.ts so the two passes are held to one invariant.
invariant: For all g, cons and opts: largestComponentFraction(polishConstrained(g, cons, opts)) >= largestComponentFraction(g), and connectedComponents(polishConstrained(g, cons, opts)).length <= connectedComponents(g).length — i.e. exactly the pair of properties `polish` is already held to, for every priorWeight.

theme: a documented generation dial that provably cannot change the output, so a user turning it gets silence
summary: `minSeparation` is extensionally inert on the entire constrained path: choosePartner sorts candidates by farness DESCENDING and then scans for the first candidate at distance >= minSep, but candidates[0] already maximises farness, so the scan can only ever return candidates[0] — the same value the fallback returns.
failure: constrainedGreedy(n, k, cons, { minSeparation: s }) returns a byte-identical edge list for s in {2,3,4,5,8,20} across all 240 configurations swept (n = 6..40 even, k in {2,3,4,5}, with sprinkled prohibitions): zero differences. The same option is re-exported as ConstrainedBuddyOptions.minSeparation on buildConstrainedBuddyGraph and is wired through app/src/panels/SettingsControls.tsx to a user-facing separation slider, so with any constraint set active a user moving that slider from 2 to 8 gets exactly the same graph, and useBuddyGraph will treat it as a settings change requiring regeneration. The existing suite cannot catch it: constrained.props.test.ts and constrained.test.ts pass `minSeparation: 5` at every call site and never vary it. (The Python reference has the identical vacuous `good or cands` at constrained_gen.py:92-93, so this is a faithful port of a reference no-op, not a divergence — the oracle will not flag it either.)
remediation: Close it by subtraction or by implementation, but not by leaving it documented as a dial. Subtraction: drop `minSeparation` from ConstrainedGreedyOptions/ConstrainedBuddyOptions (and drop the dead scan in choosePartner), state in the module header that constrained completion is unconditionally farthest-first, and have the app hide/disable the separation control when constraints are present. Implementation: mirror ringGreedy's shape — skip a vertex whose eccentricity is below the current target and demote the target when nothing qualifies — which changes outputs and so has to go through reference-python plus a fixture regeneration first.
invariant: No option declared in a public generation Options interface may be extensionally inert: for each such option there must exist inputs in its documented range for which varying it alone changes the returned edgeList(). Concretely for this one — either constrainedGreedy(n,k,cons,{minSeparation:s}) is a non-constant function of s over [1, floor(n/2)], or `minSeparation` does not appear in the exported option types.

theme: a hard-constraint guarantee stated unconditionally but enforced only by an assertion that production builds compile out
summary: checkWellFormed (the always-on precondition) mirrors only constraints.ts `structuralReasons` and the caps, omitting the required-and-prohibited check; required edges are then laid unconditionally at line 89, so under NODE_ENV=production — where assertHardConstraints is compiled out — constrainedGreedy silently returns a graph containing a prohibited edge.
failure: NODE_ENV=production, `const c = new Constraints(6); c.require(1,4).prohibit(1,4); constrainedGreedy(6, 3, c)` returns edges [[0,1],[0,2],[0,5],[1,3],[1,4],[2,3],[2,4],[3,5],[4,5]] with hasEdge(1,4) === true — a prohibited pair seated as buddies, no error, no report channel. Under the default NODE_ENV the same call throws `constrainedGreedy: prohibited edge 1–4 present`, i.e. the behaviour of a documented hard guarantee depends on an environment variable. The suite runs only in dev, so it cannot see this. buildConstrainedBuddyGraph is unaffected (it calls validate first), but constrainedGreedy is exported public API and its module header states flatly that 'prohibited edges never are' present.
remediation: Add the one missing always-on precondition to checkWellFormed: after checkConstraintIds, iterate cons.requiredPairs() and throw when cons.isProhibited(a,b) — O(#required), off the hot path, and it brings the throw-mirror genuinely 'in step' with validateDetailed as its comment claims. The postcondition then goes back to being a backstop rather than the only enforcement.
invariant: For all n, k and cons, the graph returned by constrainedGreedy either does not exist (the call threw) or contains no edge (a,b) with cons.isProhibited(a,b) — and this holds identically under NODE_ENV=production and NODE_ENV=development.

theme: a headline quality number reads 'provably optimal' for a graph whose average separation is not even defined
summary: asplGap returns 0 — its documented meaning is 'provably optimal' — whenever mooreLowerBounds yields no bound, including when the ASPL passed in is Infinity, so BuddyResult.asplGap is 0 for the degenerate rosters where BuddyResult.aspl is Infinity.
failure: buildBuddyGraph(0, 2) and buildBuddyGraph(1, 2) both return { aspl: Infinity, asplGap: 0, girth: Infinity, connected: true }. A consumer reading asplGap on its own — which is what it is exported for — reports a 0% gap, i.e. optimal, for a roster with no measurable separation at all. app/src/model.ts already defends against exactly this (`quality()` returns 0 unless Number.isFinite(aspl), with a comment saying so), which shows the hazard is understood but is being patched at each consumer instead of at the source; a second consumer of the exported asplGap would have to rediscover it. This is the same shape as the recorded 'disconnected reads as optimal' defect, one degenerate input over.
remediation: Make the guard live in the core the way `quality()` does in the app: have asplGap return NaN (or Infinity) rather than 0 when `aspl` is not finite, so 'no valid Moore bound' can never render as 'zero gap'. Ratchet it in bounds/optimizer props rather than in each consumer.
invariant: asplGap(aspl, n, k) === 0 implies Number.isFinite(aspl); equivalently, for every (n, k) accepted by buildBuddyGraph, BuddyResult.asplGap is never 0 while BuddyResult.aspl is not finite.

theme: an exported primitive performs superlinear work on a caller-supplied graph that no budget bounds, because the size/work cap lives only in the wrapper above it
summary: `boundedPolishIterations` bounds the polish LOOP but not the two full O(n*(n+m)) `allPairsSummary` sweeps that frame it (`energy(g)` before the loop at polish.ts:59, `allPairsSummary(best)` after it at polish.ts:134; `measure(g)` at constrainedGreedy.ts:155). When the budget affords ZERO iterations the call still pays both sweeps in full. This is the same shape as the anneal-calibration defect already recorded in budgets.ts ("work before the loop that the budget cannot reach is work the budget does not bound") — the calibration was moved inside the budget, the framing measurements were not.
failure: Reproduced against the built lib: `polish(ring(20000), { maxIters: 0 })` returns after 31.66 s with `result.iters === 0`; `polishConstrained(ring(20000), new Constraints(20000), { iters: 0 })` takes 15.39 s. Scaling is quadratic and confirmed (n=5000 -> 2.19s, n=10000 -> 6.75s, n=20000 -> 31.66s), so at `MAX_ROSTER` (1e6, which the `Graph` constructor permits) the same zero-iteration call is hours. `optimizer.props.test.ts`'s guard for this class states "A zero budget must buy zero work in BOTH modes" but only asserts `annealMs < hillMs + 200` — it compares the two modes to each other, so it passes while both perform unbounded work.
remediation: Compute the affordable iteration count from `input.n` and `input.numEdges()` BEFORE `input.copy()` and before the first energy/measure call. If it is 0, return the input unchanged (or throw a `too large to polish` refusal mirroring `ringGreedy`'s work cap) without any all-pairs sweep. Alternatively charge the framing sweeps against the same constant by refusing when `n * (n + m) > MAX_POLISH_WORK`. theme: an exported primitive performs superlinear work on a caller-supplied graph that no budget bounds, because the size/work cap lives only in the wrapper above it

invariant: Every exported generator entry point (`ringGreedy`, `repairDegrees`, `constrainedGreedy`) refuses — before performing any per-vertex work — any input whose modelled work exceeds its budget. Machine-checkable form: for all graphs g and all k, if `greedyWork(g.n, k) > MAX_GREEDY_WORK` then `repairDegrees(g, k)` throws, and it does so having invoked `bfsDistances` zero times.

theme: the auto-polish gate models a default iteration count that lives in a second, independently-edited copy of the constant the primitive actually uses, so the two can silently diverge on the next ordinary tuning edit

theme: constants duplicated between module and index, creating silent-drift risk when values change

invariant: Every constant that is used in multiple modules must have a single source of truth. Here, DEFAULT_POLISH_ITERS is logically tied to polish.ts and should not be redefined in index.ts; DEFAULT_CONSTRAINED_POLISH_ITERS is logically tied to constrainedGreedy.ts.

theme: iteration budget parameter has three different names across option interfaces for the same concept
summary: The iteration budget option is inconsistently named: 'polishIters' in BuddyOptions and ConstrainedBuddyOptions, but 'maxIters' in PolishOptions and 'iters' in PolishConstrainedOptions
failure: BuddyOptions.polishIters (line 88), ConstrainedBuddyOptions.polishIters (line 219), PolishOptions.maxIters (line 32 in polish.ts), and PolishConstrainedOptions.iters (line 66 in constrainedGreedy.ts) are all iteration budgets for polish passes. A caller using buildConstrainedBuddyGraph passes `polishIters`, which is converted to `iters` for polishConstrained. Rename PolishOptions.maxIters to polishIters (and update the rationale comment if it refers to the name), and rename PolishConstrainedOptions.iters to polishIters. theme: minimum separation concept called 'mind' in one generation path and 'minSeparation' in another, increasing cognitive load when extending both
summary: The minimum separation concept uses the name 'mind' in ringGreedy (and internally in buildBuddyGraph) but 'minSeparation' in constrainedGreedy, even though they are the same concept

theme: the core's auto-polish decision is k-aware but not exposed, so the app's copy of that decision is wrong and the UI states something false about what the core will do
summary: `resolveWantPolish` decides auto-polish from `polishWork(n, k, defaultIters) <= MAX_POLISH_WORK` — a function of BOTH n and k — but it is module-private and neither `polishWork` nor `MAX_POLISH_WORK` is exported from the package. `app/src/model.ts` therefore mirrors it as an n-only literal (`POLISH_MAX_N = 120`, whose comment still describes the removed `n <= 120` rule), and the two disagree in both directions. Polish is the only seed-dependent stage, so this mirror is what the reroll UI's user-facing copy is derived from.
failure: Measured with `buildBuddyGraph(n, k)` on default options: (130, 2) -> polished === true (true for all n up to ~146 at k=2, since 20000*(64+2n^2) <= 865_280_000 iff n <= 146), yet `rerollBlockReason(130, {polish:'auto'})` returns "This group is too large to shuffle — a different arrangement is only possible for smaller groups." and App.tsx's handleReroll flashes it and RETURNS without regenerating — a working feature refused with a false explanation for every roster of 121-146 people at 2 buddies (BUDDY_MIN is 2, MAX_ROSTER_N is 1000, so this is reachable from the UI). The opposite direction also reproduces: (100, 12) -> polished === false and (119, 8) -> polished === false, where `rerollBlockReason` returns null and the app promises the arrangement may vary. The pinning test app/test/reroll.test.ts:62-66 only exercises k=4, so it passes by construction and would not catch either case.
remediation: Export the gate itself from lib rather than a number the app has to re-derive: add `export function autoPolishEnabled(n: number, k: number): boolean` (the body of `resolveWantPolish`'s "auto" branch, using DEFAULT_POLISH_ITERS) to lib/src/core/index.ts and re-export it, then replace `POLISH_MAX_N` in app/src/model.ts with a call to it inside `rerollBlockReason` (and in useBuddyGraph.ts:121's force-polish guard), rewording the block copy so the k-dependent case reads correctly. Parameterize the reroll boundary test over k (at least 2, 4, 8, 12) so the k-awareness is pinned, not just one column of it.
invariant: For every (n, k) the app can generate (2 <= k <= 12, 0 <= n <= MAX_ROSTER_N), the app's predicted polish-enablement equals the core's actual one: `(rerollBlockReason(n, {...DEFAULT_SETTINGS, polish: 'auto'}) === null) === buildBuddyGraph(n, k, { polish: 'auto', polishIters: 1 }).polished`. Equivalently, once the core exports the predicate: the app contains no independent threshold for polish enablement — the app-side value is a call into the core for the same (n, k).

theme: an absent group label is treated as a shared group label, so ungrouped people get silently prohibited from each other
summary: `Constraints.fromTags` guards only against `null` (`if (ti === null) continue`) but its `tagOf` helper can return `undefined` — for any index within `tags.length` whose element is a hole or an explicit `undefined`. Since `undefined === undefined`, every pair of ungrouped people compares equal and is prohibited, directly contradicting the method's own documented contract ("Missing/out-of-range tags count as 'no group' (never grouped)"). The Python reference is correct here (`tags[i] is not None`), so this is a port defect, and the shape of the bug is invisible in the common case: the same roster expressed with a SHORTER array behaves correctly, because then `tagOf` falls through to the explicit `null`.
failure: `Constraints.fromTags(5, [1, 1, undefined, undefined, undefined]).prohibitedPairs()` returns `[[0,1],[2,3],[2,4],[3,4]]` — persons 2, 3 and 4 have no group yet are mutually prohibited. Identical result for the sparse array `const t = new Array(5); t[0]=1; t[1]=1;`. The correct answer, and what `Constraints.fromTags(5, [1, 1])` actually returns, is `[[0,1]]`. Consequences are not cosmetic: the spurious prohibited pairs shrink each ungrouped person's allowed set, can push `validate` into refusing a feasible roster via `prohibited-from-everyone` / `prohibited-splits-group` (e.g. n=4 with all four tags undefined refuses outright), and otherwise degrade ASPL. Existing tests (constrained.test.ts:271, :285) use a dense array and a short array respectively, so neither reaches the hole case.
remediation: Make `tagOf` total in the nullish sense — `const tagOf = (i: number): Tag => tags[i] ?? null;` (which also subsumes the `i < tags.length` branch) — and/or change the guard to `if (ti == null) continue;`. Add a test asserting the invariant above for a sparse array and for explicit `undefined` entries.
invariant: For all n and all tag arrays, normalizing absent entries must not change the output: `Constraints.fromTags(n, tags).prohibitedPairs()` deep-equals `Constraints.fromTags(n, Array.from({length: n}, (_, i) => tags[i] ?? null)).prohibitedPairs()`. Equivalently: (i, j) is prohibited by fromTags iff `tagOf(i) != null && tagOf(i) === tagOf(j)`.

theme: a cost gate that only bounds the loop, while the unconditional work around the loop stays unbounded in the input size
summary: `polish` and `polishConstrained` have a work cap but no size cap, and pay two-to-three full Theta(n*(n+m)) all-pairs sweeps plus two graph copies before and after the loop that `boundedPolishIterations` is the sole gate on — so a call the budget prices at ZERO iterations still runs for minutes.
failure: Measured: `polish(ring(40000), { mode: "hill", maxIters: 0 })` -> boundedPolishIterations(40000, 40000, 0, 20000) === 0, function returns iters:0, wall time 160,246 ms. Sibling: `polishConstrained(ring(30000), new Constraints(30000), { iters: 0 })` -> bounded iters 0, 47,770 ms (n=10000 -> 3,780 ms). Cost scales as n^2 and `Graph` admits n up to MAX_ROSTER = 1e6, so `polish(new Graph(1e6))` extrapolates to ~10^5 s. The work comes from `energy(g)` at polish.ts:64, `best = g.copy()` at :65, `allPairsSummary(best)` at :139, and the mirror set in polishConstrained (`input.edgeList()` :148, `input.copy()` :163, `measure(g)` :164, `g.copy()` :168) — none of them reachable by the budget. Reachability: through the library's public API (both are exported from index.ts:36/50); NOT through the current app UI, whose only large-graph producer, importGraph, caps n at 1000, and whose in-app polish callers are bounded by MAX_CACHED_N/MAX_CONSTRAINED_N. This is the same defect class the repo already fixed one boundary over (`polish(ring(20), {maxIters: Infinity})` never returned) — the sibling is the graph SIZE rather than the iteration COUNT, and the ratcheted test for it, optimizer.props.test.ts:377 "A zero budget must buy zero work in BOTH modes", asserts only that anneal is within 200 ms of hill at n=300, so it passes while the absolute cost is unbounded.

That closes the theme rather than the case: the guard is stated in terms of the sweep cost the function actually pays, so it covers the pre-loop sweeps, the post-loop `allPairsSummary(best)`, the copies and the anneal calibration together, at every n, for any options object.
invariant: For every Graph g and every options object, `polish(g, opts)` and `polishConstrained(g, cons, opts)` either throw before performing any all-pairs sweep, or complete having performed at most a bounded multiple of MAX_POLISH_WORK operations. Machine-checkable form: for all g, if boundedPolishIterations(g.n, g.edgeList().length, opts.maxIters ?? opts.iters, DEFAULT) === 0 then the call throws (it must not run a sweep it cannot afford an iteration of); and for all g and opts where it does not throw, elapsed time is bounded by a constant independent of g.n.

theme: a cost gate that only bounds the loop, while the unconditional work around the loop stays unbounded in the input size
summary: `refusedResult` allocates an n-sized array of arrays sized against MAX_ROSTER (1e6) rather than against the largest roster the constrained builder can actually accept (MAX_CONSTRAINED_N = 5000), so refusing an oversized roster costs 200x more allocation than accepting the biggest legal one.

The guard's own comment at index.ts:465-466 states the intent — 'A malformed/oversized n reaches here (that IS what's being refused), so never allocate an n-sized array from it' — but the size clamp uses MAX_ROSTER, and 1e6 IS oversized for this entry point. On a main thread that is a quarter-second of jank plus 44 MB handed back for an input that was refused.
remediation: Clamp the placeholder allocation to the largest roster this builder can accept (MAX_CONSTRAINED_N), not to MAX_ROSTER — or return an empty `buddies` on every refusal, since the documented contract already tells callers to read `report.refusals` first and the metric fields are placeholders. Accepted inputs (n <= 5000) are unaffected either way.
invariant: For every n, the value returned by buildConstrainedBuddyGraph on a refused input satisfies buddies.length <= MAX_CONSTRAINED_N — no refusal ever allocates more than the largest roster the builder would accept.

theme: F9's soft-preservation seam (priorWeight/priorHard) is entirely routed through polishConstrained; the unrelated general-purpose auto-polish cost gate (resolveWantPolish/MAX_POLISH_WORK) silently turns priors into a complete no-op above a roster size the gate doesn't know priors exist at, and ConstraintReport gives no dedicated signal that this happened
summary: buildConstrainedBuddyGraph only applies priorWeight when `resolveWantPolish` (n,k-only) decides to run polish at all. Above roughly n≈190 at k=4 (polishWork(n,k,DEFAULT_CONSTRAINED_POLISH_ITERS) > MAX_POLISH_WORK), the default 'auto' entry point never reaches constrainedMeasure's prior-penalty term, so cons.addPrior(...) has zero effect on the output — yet report.priorsKeptFraction still reports a plausible-looking number (purely incidental survival from constrainedGreedy, which never looks at priors at all), and the only hint anything is different is the generic `polished: false` flag, which exists for unrelated reasons and isn't documented as a proxy for 'were priors even attempted'.
failure: Reproduced in .review-scratch/priors_no_polish.mjs: n=300, k=4, a Constraints with every ring pair (i,(i+1)%n) added as a prior via addPrior. buildConstrainedBuddyGraph(300, 4, cons, {polish:'auto'}) returns polished:false and report.priorsKeptFraction: 0.51 — a number indistinguishable, from the report shape alone, from a real (if partial) preservation outcome. A UI following the plan's own copy ('report shows "kept 46 of 50 pairs"') would show a specific, confident-looking number for a run where the preservation mechanism never ran at all.
remediation: Either (a) add an explicit report field (e.g. `priorsAttempted: boolean`, true iff polish ran AND priorWeight!=0) so a consumer can distinguish 'priors were weighed and this many survived' from 'priors never had a chance', or (b) make resolveWantPolish's decision aware of whether priors are present (e.g. it is the one case with a real, if modest, quality payoff even outside the general ASPL-only budget, so it could warrant a smaller but nonzero iteration allowance rather than a hard off). Either change is local to index.ts/budgets.ts.
invariant: For every (n,k,cons) with cons.priorCount>0, ConstraintReport must let a caller distinguish 'priors were weighed by polish this run' from 'priors could not be weighed because auto-polish was gated off' without cross-referencing the (n,k)-dependent MAX_POLISH_WORK budget themselves; currently both cases produce a priorsKeptFraction computed the same way and neither is flagged.

theme: comment references function in wrong module, sending contributor to look in wrong place

theme: public interface document claims default value for an option that is never applied and whose value is silently ignored
summary: ConstrainedBuddyOptions.minSeparation documents a 'Default 5' that is not applied, and the value is ignored by the constrained path anyway

But: (a) no default is applied—if omitted, undefined is passed (line 313); (b) constrainedGreedy.ts lines 56–62 explicitly document that minSeparation is 'ACCEPTED AND IGNORED'; (c) the comment claims it 'aims for' a value when choosePartner maximizes separation greedily without a target. Accepted for API compatibility; the constrained path maximises separation greedily and ignores this value. **/'

theme: the option value the algorithm actually acts on and the value the report is derived from are computed in two independent places, so a value one of them normalizes away is still counted by the other
summary: A non-finite `priorWeight` is silently coerced to 0 inside `polishConstrained` (so priors are never weighed) while `buildConstrainedBuddyGraph` still counts it as `priorWeight !== 0` and therefore reports a numeric `priorsKeptFraction` — the exact 'meaningless coincidental number' the field's own doc comment says it must return `null` for.
failure:
n=30, k=4, 15 prior pairs, `buildConstrainedBuddyGraph(30, 4, cons, { priorWeight: NaN })` (and `Infinity`) returns `report.priorsKeptFraction === 0.5333…`, byte-identical to the `priorWeight: 0` run — which correctly returns `null`. Reproduced in .review-scratch/p2.mjs:
  w=0        reported=null   actual=0.5333
  w=NaN      reported=0.5333 actual=0.5333   <-- lies
  w=Infinity reported=0.5333 actual=0.5333   <-- lies
  w=2        reported=1      actual=1
An organizer reading 'Infinity weight -> 53% of prior buddies kept' cannot tell that from 'priors were honoured to the tune of 53%'; in fact priors were never consulted, and `priorWeight: Infinity` — a caller asking for maximal preservation — silently gets none. index.ts:351-353 resolves the weight, constrainedGreedy.ts:165 re-resolves it differently, and index.ts:383 derives `priorsWeighed` from the first.
remediation: Resolve the effective weight ONCE and let both the polish call and the report read that single value. Concretely, in `buildConstrainedBuddyGraph` compute `priorWeight = Number.isFinite(w) ? w : 0` before the `polishConstrained` call (or export a `resolvePriorWeight` from constrainedGreedy.ts and use it on both sides), so `Number.isFinite` cannot be applied on one side of the boundary and not the other. Close the sibling in the same edit: `polished: true` is likewise reported from the caller's intent rather than from the iteration count `boundedPolishIterations` actually granted, so `polishIters: 0` reports a pass that never ran.
invariant: For all n, k, cons and all w with `!Number.isFinite(w)`, `buildConstrainedBuddyGraph(n, k, cons, { priorWeight: w })` is observationally identical to the same call with `priorWeight: 0` — in particular `report.priorsKeptFraction === null` whenever `!cons.priorHard` and the weight the polish objective actually used is not a finite non-zero number.

theme: a hard guarantee is asserted only where it cannot be enforced, so the guarantee is silently false in production and misattributed in development
summary: `polishConstrained` never adds edges and never checks that its INPUT already satisfies the constraints, yet the module header promises 'both guarantee the hard constraints'; the only check is the dev-mode postcondition, so under NODE_ENV=production a violating input is returned unchanged and unflagged, and in dev the error blames `polishConstrained` for the caller's defect.
failure:
n=8, ring graph, `cons.require(0,5)` (absent) and `cons.prohibit(1,2)` (present). Reproduced in .review-scratch/p7.mjs:
  $ node p7.mjs                  -> threw: 'polishConstrained: prohibited edge 1–2 present'
  $ NODE_ENV=production node p7.mjs -> returned. required present? false  prohibited present? true
So the same public API call either throws a misattributed error or silently returns a graph containing a prohibited pair and missing a required one, depending on an environment variable. `checkConstraintIds` (constrainedGreedy.ts:150) already establishes the always-on precondition style for this function; it checks id ranges but not constraint satisfaction.
remediation: Add the input check to the always-on precondition block beside `checkConstraintIds`: refuse an input graph that already contains a prohibited pair or is missing a required one, with a message naming the pair and pointing at `constrainedGreedy`. It is O(#constraints), the same cost class as the checks already there, and it turns an environment-dependent silent breach into one deterministic refusal. Keep the dev-mode postcondition — with the precondition in place it once again asserts something `polishConstrained` is actually responsible for.
invariant: For every `Graph g` and `Constraints c`, `polishConstrained(g, c, opts)` either throws or returns a graph that contains every pair in `c.requiredPairs()` and none in `c.prohibitedPairs()` — and which branch it takes does not depend on `process.env.NODE_ENV`.

theme: numeric options are validated inconsistently at the entry point, so a non-numeric value silently disables a comparison-based rule instead of being refused, and can surface as NaN in a reported metric
summary: `buildBuddyGraph`/`ringGreedy` validate `n` and `k` but accept any `minSeparation`; `NaN` makes `ecc < curMind` always false, silently disabling the separation target (a different graph, not an ignored option) and propagating into the returned `finalMinSeparation`.
failure: Reproduced in .review-scratch/p11.mjs. Across n=3..60 x k in {2,3,4,5} with `polish: false`, `buildBuddyGraph(n, k, { minSeparation: NaN })` returns a DIFFERENT edge set from the default in 45 of 232 configurations — e.g. buildBuddyGraph(6,4): aspl 1.4 girth 4 (default) vs aspl 1.2667 girth 3 (NaN). And `buildBuddyGraph(1, 2, { minSeparation: NaN }).finalMinSeparation` and `buildBuddyGraph(2, 2, ...)` are both `NaN` (JSON.stringify renders them as `null`), because `Math.min(NaN, floor(n/2))` is NaN and the `Number.isFinite(gi)` fallback at index.ts:207 hands that raw value straight out. This is the untreated sibling of a defect already fixed one line away: ringGreedy.ts:46 validates `k` with the comment '`deg >= NaN` is always false, silently disabling the degree-cap logic' — the identical NaN-comparison hazard for `mind` was left open.
remediation: Validate `mind` where `k` is already validated in `ringGreedy`: refuse a `minSeparation` that is not a non-negative integer with the same style of message ('minimum separation X must be a non-negative integer'), so the unconstrained builder's stated 'malformed input throws a clear error' contract covers every numeric option rather than two of three. `finalMinSeparation` then cannot be NaN by construction, and no separate clamp is needed at index.ts:207.
invariant: No numeric field of a returned `BuddyResult` or `ConstrainedBuddyResult` is NaN for any input the builder does not throw on or refuse; equivalently, `buildBuddyGraph` throws on a `minSeparation` that is not a non-negative integer, exactly as it already does for such a `k`.

theme: a cost gate charges for one unit of the expensive step while the code performs several, so an input the budget prices at ~1 iteration still burns minutes of synchronous main-thread time
summary: `checkPolishSize` is calibrated so that ONE `allPairsSummary` sweep fits `MAX_POLISH_WORK` ("a single sweep must fit the same MAX_POLISH_WORK the whole loop is held to, which is the tightest bound that cannot refuse a configuration the loop itself would have accepted"). But `polish` performs the initial `energy(g)`, up to `min(100, maxIters)` anneal-calibration evaluations, `maxIters` loop evaluations, and a final `allPairsSummary(best)` — and `boundedPolishIterations` divides the SAME budget by the SAME per-sweep cost, so the loop alone is allowed a full budget on top of the fixed sweeps. Total admitted work is therefore ~4x `MAX_POLISH_WORK`, not 1x. `polishConstrained` has the same shape (start measure + final assertions outside the loop). Both are exported public API, which is the module's own stated reason for putting the bound inside them rather than in a wrapper.
failure: `polish(ring(20000), { mode: "anneal" })` — measured. `checkPolishSize(20000, 20000)` computes sweep = 8.00e8 <= MAX_POLISH_WORK (8.653e8) and admits it; `boundedPolishIterations` prices the call at **1 iteration**. The call then runs for **74.8 s** synchronously (one `allPairsSummary` on that graph is 18.8 s; the call performs four of them plus two graph copies). Nothing refuses it and nothing warns. The same gate admits `polishConstrained(ring(20000), new Constraints(20000), { iters: 0 })` — priced at ZERO iterations — for **18.4 s**; the docstring cites the 30000-vertex version of exactly this call at 48 s as the defect `checkPolishSize` was added to close, so the fix moved the number down rather than removing the class. Mid-range confirmation of the multiplier: at n=8000 (sweep 1.28e8, 6 iterations afforded) `polish(anneal)` runs 31.6 s against 2.6 s for a single sweep — 14 sweeps for a budget that pays for 6.
remediation: Charge the out-of-loop work in the gate and deduct it from the loop's allowance, so the accept-set is defined by the total. Concretely: give `budgets.ts` a `FIXED_POLISH_SWEEPS` constant (3 for `polish`: initial energy, final summary, and the copies; 2 for `polishConstrained`), have `checkPolishSize` refuse when `FIXED_POLISH_SWEEPS * n * (n + m) > MAX_POLISH_WORK`, and have `boundedPolishIterations` divide `MAX_POLISH_WORK - FIXED_POLISH_SWEEPS * perIteration` (floored at 0) rather than the whole budget — with the anneal calibration drawn from that same remaining allowance instead of getting its own `min(100, maxIters)` pool. Re-derive the constant so the pinned k=4 boundary (`polishWork(120,4,20000)` admitted, 121 not) does not move.
invariant: For every `(graph, options)` that `polish` / `polishConstrained` do not refuse, the total number of full all-pairs evaluations they perform (instrumentable as a counter around `allPairsSummary`) multiplied by the per-sweep cost `n*(n+m)` must be <= `MAX_POLISH_WORK`. Equivalently: a call that is admitted never costs more than the budget it was gated on, at any n, m, mode or iteration request — including calls priced at 0 or 1 iterations.

theme: one untrusted number from the settings object is sanitized by the consumer that acts on it but read raw by the code that reports what happened, so a hostile value turns "not measured" into a fabricated measurement
summary: `buildConstrainedBuddyGraph` computes `priorWeight` from `options.priorWeight` WITHOUT finiteness checking, hands it to `polishConstrained` (which does check: `Number.isFinite(opts.priorWeight) ? ... : 0`), and then decides whether priors were weighed with `polished && priorWeight !== 0` using the RAW value. For any non-finite or non-numeric `priorWeight`, the optimizer uses weight 0 — priors are never in the objective — while the report satisfies `priorWeight !== 0` and emits a number. That is precisely the case `ConstraintReport.priorsKeptFraction`'s own doc says must be `null` ("whatever fraction happened to survive was pure coincidence... `null` already means 'not measured'"). The existing test `a non-finite priorWeight does not silently disable the pass` asserts the intended invariant (`withNaN.edges` equals `withZero.edges`) but stops at `edges`, so the report field escapes it.
failure: `buildConstrainedBuddyGraph(20, 4, consWithPriors, { polish: true, priorWeight: JSON.parse('{"w":1e999}').w })` (i.e. `Infinity`, the only way a hostile JSON settings object can express it) returns `report.priorsKeptFraction === 0.3`, identical in graph and in fact to the `priorWeight: 0` call — which correctly returns `null`. Measured for `NaN`, `Infinity`, `-Infinity`, `1e999`-from-JSON and the string `"3"`: every one reports 0.3 where the honest answer is `null`, and the actual surviving-prior fraction (0.3) is the untouched coincidence value. A caller reading "30% of prior buddies kept" cannot tell it from "priors were honoured to the tune of 30%".
remediation: Sanitize once, at the boundary, and let both readers see the same number: in `buildConstrainedBuddyGraph`, resolve `priorWeight` through the same `Number.isFinite(...) ? ... : 0` rule before passing it to `polishConstrained` (or have `polishConstrained` return the effective weight it used), so `buildReport`'s `priorsWeighed` argument is derived from the weight the optimizer actually applied. Extend the existing test at `lib/test/optimizer.props.test.ts:481` from `edges` to the whole result.
invariant: For every `w` with `!Number.isFinite(w)`, `buildConstrainedBuddyGraph(n, k, cons, { ...opts, priorWeight: w })` must deep-equal the same call with `priorWeight: 0` — the whole result, `report.priorsKeptFraction` included, not just `edges`. More generally: `report.priorsKeptFraction` is non-null only when the weight the objective actually used was finite and non-zero (or priors were promoted via `priorHard`).

theme: False comment about when constraint metrics are meaningful
summary: Comment claims priorsKeptFraction is only meaningful when polish runs with non-zero weight, but code allows it when priors are promoted to hard regardless of polish status.
failure: buildConstrainedBuddyGraph(30, 4, cons_with_priorHard=true, no_polish_options) returns report.priorsKeptFraction=1.0, contradicting comment that says 'only meaningful when polish ran and weight non-zero'. Test constrained.test.ts:380 confirms this case: sets priorHard=true, no polish option passed, expects priorsKeptFraction=1.
remediation: Replace lines 345-347 comment with accurate description: 'Hoisted because priorsKeptFraction meaningfulness depends on whether priors were ACCOUNTED FOR — either promoted to hard or soft-weighted by polish. See the comment below (lines 378-382) which correctly describes all three cases.'
invariant: priorsWeighed === (active.priorHard || (polished && priorWeight !== 0)). When priorsWeighed is true and priors exist, priorsKeptFraction is calculated, not null. This holds whether priors are hard or soft-weighted.

theme: Misleading complexity analysis in comment about pre-loop work
summary: Comment claims 'both are Theta(n·(n+m))' when comparing copy and energy operations, but Graph.copy() is O(n+m), not Theta(n·(n+m)).
failure: Comment states both operations are Theta(n·(n+m)), but Graph.copy() (lines 112-118 in graph.ts) iterates adjacency list once: for each vertex loop all edges, which is O(n+m). In contrast, allPairsSummary (metrics.ts) calls BFS from each vertex: O(n·(n+m)). For a graph with n=40000, m=50000: copy ≈2.25M operations, energy ≈3.6e12 operations.
remediation: Clarify that checkPolishSize bounds the dominant allPairsSummary term. Change to: 'BEFORE the copy and before energy(), which is the costly part: allPairsSummary is Theta(n·(n+m)) and unreachable by the iteration budget below, so a call priced at zero iterations still ran for 160 s at n=40000.'
invariant: Graph.copy() time complexity is O(n + m) where m is edge count. For sparse graphs where m ≈ O(n), this is negligible compared to allPairsSummary which is Theta(n²) or worse.

theme: every generation entry point is supposed to carry both a size cap and a work cap, but one exported generator validates its degree parameter not at all
summary: `repairDegrees(g, k, minDist)` is exported public API and performs no validation of `k` (not even `Number.isInteger`) and enforces no work budget, so a caller-supplied huge `k` drives it to build a near-complete graph one BFS-scan at a time; `ringGreedy` refuses the identical (n, k) pair via `MAX_GREEDY_WORK`.
failure: Measured in /home/user/ringweave/.review-scratch/p10.mjs: repairDegrees(ring(200), 1e9) = 544 ms, ring(300) = 2085 ms, ring(400) = 5642 ms (~n^3.4), extrapolating to hours at n=5000 which MAX_ROSTER (1e6) admits. greedyWork(400, 1e9) = 1.28e10 already exceeds MAX_GREEDY_WORK = 1e10, i.e. ringGreedy(400, 1e9) throws 'too large to generate in reasonable time' while repairDegrees(ring(400), 1e9) runs to completion. repairDegrees(g, NaN) and repairDegrees(g, Infinity) are likewise accepted silently (NaN makes `degree(v) < k` false everywhere, so the pass is a silent no-op rather than a refusal — the same silent-no-op failure mode already fixed for `mind` in ringGreedy and for `priorWeight` in polishConstrained).
remediation: Give `repairDegrees` the same two guards its sibling generators already carry, at the top of the function: reject a non-integer or negative `k` with the wording `ringGreedy` uses, and throw when `greedyWork(g.n, k) > MAX_GREEDY_WORK`. `budgets.ts` already exports both; this is three lines and no new constant. Closing the theme means checking the sibling: `girth` is documented as deliberately uncapped because its cost is fixed by the caller's own Graph, which is a different (and defensible) case — `repairDegrees` differs precisely because its cost is driven by an unvalidated caller-supplied parameter.
invariant: For every graph `g` and every `k`, `repairDegrees(g, k)` either returns having done work bounded by the same budget its only in-tree caller is held to, or throws — machine-checkable as: `repairDegrees(g, k)` throws whenever `!Number.isInteger(k) || k < 0 || greedyWork(g.n, k) > MAX_GREEDY_WORK`, and otherwise returns; equivalently, no (g, k) accepted by `repairDegrees` is refused by `ringGreedy` for the same (n, k).

theme: the generation work budget is not an upper bound on the work it claims to bound — its cost estimator changes shape with k, so the worst input the budget admits does roughly twice the work the budget prices it at
summary: `greedyWork(n,k) = n²·(n·min(k,n-1)/2)` is calibrated at k=4 and is NOT proportional to the operations ringGreedy actually performs. It charges for every edge in a k-regular graph, but the ring seed already supplies n of them, and it does not model that `findPair`'s per-call scan stays ~2n² for dense k while it collapses as vertices saturate at sparse k. The result is that the ratio (real operations / budget) rises from ~1.06 at the calibration point to ~2.34 at the worst admitted configuration, so MAX_GREEDY_WORK admits inputs costing over twice what the constant's own documentation says it buys. This is the primary DoS gate for attacker-chosen (n,k) on the unconstrained path.
failure:
Measured with an operation counter instrumented into a compiled copy of greedy.ts (distance-cache cell writes in `updateAfterEdge` + candidate scans in `findPair`), so the evidence is machine-independent:
  buildBuddyGraph(1000, 4)  -> budget 2.00e9, ops 2.12e9  (ratio 1.06), 6.9 s
  buildBuddyGraph(1000, 20) -> budget 1.00e10, ops 2.19e10 (ratio 2.19), 136.7 s
  buildBuddyGraph(800, 39)  -> budget 9.98e9, ops 2.34e10 (ratio 2.34), 215.7 s
All three are ACCEPTED (greedyWork <= MAX_GREEDY_WORK = 1e10). buildBuddyGraph(800, 39) with default options runs 220.8 s wall-clock against a constant documented as "1e10 is therefore ~60 s worst case"; correcting for this machine's measured ~1.7x factor (established independently against the constrained-path table, which reproduces uniformly) that is still ~130 s, i.e. ~2.2x the stated ceiling. The app-reachable ceiling (1000, 12) measured 67.1 s against a documented 38.5 s. Note the worst case is NOT at either end of the k range the comment's table samples — (500,160) is 55.3 s and (376,375) is 22.0 s — so the table's sampling is what hid it.
remediation: Make the estimator shape-correct rather than lowering the constant (lowering it alone would refuse (1000,12), which ships). Charge the edges ACTUALLY added and the real per-edge scan: `greedyWork(n,k) = 3·n²·max(0, n·min(k,n-1)/2 − n)`. Against the three measured points that estimator has ratios 0.71 / 0.81 / 0.82 — flat to within 15% instead of varying 2.2x. Then recalibrate MAX_GREEDY_WORK to the tightest value that still admits (1000,12), and restate the wall-clock claim from the recalibrated worst point rather than from k=4. Ratchet with an instrumented-counter property test rather than a timing test.
invariant: For every integer (n,k) that `ringGreedy` admits (i.e. n <= MAX_CACHED_N and greedyWork(n,k) <= MAX_GREEDY_WORK), the number of inner-loop operations the run actually performs — distance-cache cell writes in `updateAfterEdge` plus candidate-scan steps in `findPair` — must be <= MAX_GREEDY_WORK. Equivalently: greedyWork must dominate the operation count it is named for, for all admitted inputs, not only at the calibration point. Today (800,39) violates this at 2.34e10 > 1e10.

theme: an untrusted vertex index reaches an exported metric that has no bounds guard, producing a native TypeError instead of the module's own clear refusal
summary: `metrics.ts` defines `checkVertex` precisely because "the path/eccentricity entry points take indices chosen by a caller (ultimately a user selection), and `bfsDistances` would silently tolerate a bad one" — but `bfsDistances` is itself exported from the package index (index.ts line 16) and is the only vertex-index-taking export that does NOT call it. `shortestPath` and `eccentricity` both do. An out-of-range source makes `dist[s] = 0` a no-op on the Int32Array, then `g.adj[u]` is `undefined` and the for-of throws a TypeError that names neither the bad index nor the valid range.
failure: bfsDistances(ring(10), -1) / (…, 10) / (…, 2.5) / (…, NaN) / (…, 1e9) all throw `TypeError: g.adj[u] is not iterable`, instead of the module's own `source -1 must be an integer in [0, 9]`. Not a hang and not a memory-safety issue — a diagnosis-quality failure on the one exported metric whose sibling exports are guarded. No caller in app/src today (the app uses `shortestPath`/`eccentricity`), so this is forward-looking rather than presently reachable.
remediation: Add `checkVertex(g, s, "source")` as the first statement of `bfsDistances`. It is O(1) and the function already allocates an Int32Array(n), so it cannot be on a hot path where the check matters. `girth`'s internal per-source loop and `allPairsSummary` pass loop indices and are unaffected.
invariant: Every exported function in metrics.ts that accepts a vertex index rejects a non-integer or out-of-range index with the module's `<label> <v> must be an integer in [0, n-1]` Error, for all graphs and all index values — no exported metric may surface a native TypeError or return a distance vector derived from an index it never validated.

theme: a size/shape gate that cannot run because the expensive step happens inside the constructor that precedes it — fromTags builds O(n²) prohibited pairs before validate exists to refuse them, and validates no n at all
summary: Re-verifying the limitation already recorded in lib/CLAUDE.md, because it is exactly the shape this lens is asked to hunt and the numbers had not been re-measured. `Constraints.fromTags` takes `n` on faith — `degreeOf` in the same file, the `Graph` constructor and `validate` all guard it — and then runs an unguarded double loop that materializes one Set key per same-tag pair. Every gate that could refuse the input (MAX_CONSTRAINED_N, MAX_CONSTRAINED_WORK) lives in `validate`, which by construction runs after the constructor has already paid. Filed as deferral, not blocking: `grep -rn fromTags app/src` is empty, so nothing untrusted reaches it in the current tree.
failure: Measured against the compiled lib: `Constraints.fromTags(3000, new Array(3000).fill('A'))` builds 4,498,500 prohibited-pair keys in 4,958 ms before returning — `validate` never gets a turn, and at tens of millions of pairs the Set construction itself is the failure. `Constraints.fromTags(-5, [])` and `Constraints.fromTags(2.5, [])` both return without throwing, where `new Graph(-5)` and `degreeOf(-5, …)` refuse. `Constraints.fromTags(4, [NaN, NaN, NaN, NaN])` yields prohibitedCount 0: NaN !== NaN, so a NaN tag silently inverts the documented `prohibit_same` policy rather than grouping.
remediation: When a tag UI (F7) lands: validate `n` against MAX_ROSTER/MAX_CONSTRAINED_N as the first statement, then pre-count group sizes in one O(n) pass and refuse against an explicit pair cap (sum of C(size,2) over groups) BEFORE entering the double loop, and coerce non-finite tag values to null so they take the documented "never grouped" path. Until then, keep it out of any untrusted call path.
invariant: `Constraints.fromTags` allocates no more than O(n) before it has validated n and refused against an explicit prohibited-pair cap; and for all tag arrays, a tag value that is not equal to itself (NaN) is treated identically to null (never grouped) rather than never matching.

theme: the flagship committed feature (F9, minimal-disruption recalc) has no implementation path on the core's default/fast tier — prior-preservation exists only on the weaker constrained tier
summary: buildBuddyGraph/polish (the ring-greedy-seeded, Moore-optimal default tier) has no priors/history concept anywhere in its option surface or objective; the only prior-preservation machinery (Constraints.addPrior/priorHard, polishConstrained's priorWeight term, DEFAULT_PRIOR_WEIGHT) lives on buildConstrainedBuddyGraph/constrainedGreedy, which the churn-priors-weight.md benchmark that grounds the F9 product claim already builds on exclusively. So any future 'recalculate, preserve buddies' implementation must route through the constrained tier even for a roster with zero hard constraints, permanently losing girth/asplGap (documented as omitted from ConstrainedBuddyResult because Moore's bound assumes a k-regular target constrained graphs only approximate) and changing the result shape for that roster from that point on.
failure: a roster that has never used F7 constraints gets 'preserve buddies' toggled on for one recalc (F9): the app has no way to ask buildBuddyGraph/polish to weight toward the previous edge set, so it must call buildConstrainedBuddyGraph with an all-priors Constraints object instead — the returned ConstraintReport-shaped result has no girth/asplGap, and the underlying algorithm silently changes from ring-greedy (near-Moore-optimal by construction) to constrainedGreedy (general-purpose, ~28% incidental prior retention before polish per the churn benchmark) for that roster going forward
remediation: when F9 implementation actually starts (M4), decide explicitly whether the unconstrained tier gains its own lightweight prior-bias (e.g. a priorWeight/priorPairs option threaded into polish()'s objective, mirroring constrainedMeasure) or whether F9 is documented as always promoting a roster onto the constrained tier the first time 'preserve buddies' is used — and record whichever choice in lib/CLAUDE.md's known-limitations list, since it is not currently written down there (only app/CLAUDE.md notes the app-side wiring is missing, not this core-shape consequence)
invariant: for every call site requesting prior-weighted generation (a set of pairs to softly preserve), reachability requires ConstrainedBuddyOptions/Constraints — grep for priorWeight|addPrior|priorHard across lib/src/core/{index,polish}.ts confirms zero occurrences outside constrainedGreedy.ts/constraints.ts/index.ts's constrained branch — this holds today and will only stop holding once someone deliberately changes it

theme: public API surface type safety violation where TypeScript type allows values the implementation rejects at runtime
summary: TagPolicy type declares 'require_same' as valid, but Constraints.fromTags() throws 'unknown tag policy' when called with it
failure: Constraints.fromTags(5, [1,1,2], 'require_same') — TypeScript: accepted as type-safe. Runtime: throws Error('unknown tag policy require_same')
remediation: Implement the 'require_same' case in the fromTags() switch statement (lines 114–126) by adding a case that calls c.require(i,j) for same-tag pairs, mirroring the prohibit_same logic. Alternatively, if require_same is deferred, remove it from the TagPolicy type union (line 46) and document in lib/CLAUDE.md known-limitations under the fromTags entry.
