theme: a size/shape gate that cannot run because the expensive step happens inside the constructor that precedes it — fromTags builds O(n²) prohibited pairs before validate exists to refuse them, and validates no n at all
summary: Re-verifying the limitation already recorded in lib/CLAUDE.md, because it is exactly the shape this lens is asked to hunt and the numbers had not been re-measured. `Constraints.fromTags` takes `n` on faith — `degreeOf` in the same file, the `Graph` constructor and `validate` all guard it — and then runs an unguarded double loop that materializes one Set key per same-tag pair. Every gate that could refuse the input (MAX_CONSTRAINED_N, MAX_CONSTRAINED_WORK) lives in `validate`, which by construction runs after the constructor has already paid. Filed as deferral, not blocking: `grep -rn fromTags app/src` is empty, so nothing untrusted reaches it in the current tree.
failure: Measured against the compiled lib: `Constraints.fromTags(3000, new Array(3000).fill('A'))` builds 4,498,500 prohibited-pair keys in 4,958 ms before returning — `validate` never gets a turn, and at tens of millions of pairs the Set construction itself is the failure. `Constraints.fromTags(-5, [])` and `Constraints.fromTags(2.5, [])` both return without throwing, where `new Graph(-5)` and `degreeOf(-5, …)` refuse. `Constraints.fromTags(4, [NaN, NaN, NaN, NaN])` yields prohibitedCount 0: NaN !== NaN, so a NaN tag silently inverts the documented `prohibit_same` policy rather than grouping.
remediation: When a tag UI (F7) lands: validate `n` against MAX_ROSTER/MAX_CONSTRAINED_N as the first statement, then pre-count group sizes in one O(n) pass and refuse against an explicit pair cap (sum of C(size,2) over groups) BEFORE entering the double loop, and coerce non-finite tag values to null so they take the documented "never grouped" path. Until then, keep it out of any untrusted call path.
invariant: `Constraints.fromTags` allocates no more than O(n) before it has validated n and refused against an explicit prohibited-pair cap; and for all tag arrays, a tag value that is not equal to itself (NaN) is treated identically to null (never grouped) rather than never matching.

theme: the flagship committed feature (F9, minimal-disruption recalc) has no implementation path on the core's default/fast tier — prior-preservation exists only on the weaker constrained tier
summary: buildBuddyGraph/polish (the ring-greedy-seeded, Moore-optimal default tier) has no priors/history concept anywhere in its option surface or objective; the only prior-preservation machinery (Constraints.addPrior/priorHard, polishConstrained's priorWeight term, DEFAULT_PRIOR_WEIGHT) lives on buildConstrainedBuddyGraph/constrainedGreedy, which the churn-priors-weight.md benchmark that grounds the F9 product claim already builds on exclusively. So any future 'recalculate, preserve buddies' implementation must route through the constrained tier even for a roster with zero hard constraints, permanently losing girth/asplGap (documented as omitted from ConstrainedBuddyResult because Moore's bound assumes a k-regular target constrained graphs only approximate) and changing the result shape for that roster from that point on.
failure: a roster that has never used F7 constraints gets 'preserve buddies' toggled on for one recalc (F9): the app has no way to ask buildBuddyGraph/polish to weight toward the previous edge set, so it must call buildConstrainedBuddyGraph with an all-priors Constraints object instead — the returned ConstraintReport-shaped result has no girth/asplGap, and the underlying algorithm silently changes from ring-greedy (near-Moore-optimal by construction) to constrainedGreedy (general-purpose, ~28% incidental prior retention before polish per the churn benchmark) for that roster going forward
remediation: when F9 implementation actually starts (M4), decide explicitly whether the unconstrained tier gains its own lightweight prior-bias (e.g. a priorWeight/priorPairs option threaded into polish()'s objective, mirroring constrainedMeasure) or whether F9 is documented as always promoting a roster onto the constrained tier the first time 'preserve buddies' is used — and record whichever choice in lib/CLAUDE.md's known-limitations list, since it is not currently written down there (only app/CLAUDE.md notes the app-side wiring is missing, not this core-shape consequence)
invariant: for every call site requesting prior-weighted generation (a set of pairs to softly preserve), reachability requires ConstrainedBuddyOptions/Constraints — grep for priorWeight|addPrior|priorHard across lib/src/core/{index,polish}.ts confirms zero occurrences outside constrainedGreedy.ts/constraints.ts/index.ts's constrained branch — this holds today and will only stop holding once someone deliberately changes it

theme: two sources of roster size (the `n` parameter and `cons.n`) can disagree, so the guard that enforces the degree cap silently no-ops and a hard guarantee is broken without an error
summary: `checkWellFormed` validates constraint endpoints against the parameter `n` but reads the required-degree vector from `cons.requiredDegree()`, which is sized by `cons.n`; when `cons.n < n` the vector has holes for the very vertices being checked, `undefined > k` is false, and the documented "required-degree over k" refusal never fires — so `constrainedGreedy` returns a graph exceeding k in production builds where the postcondition is compiled out.
failure: NODE_ENV=production; `const c = new Constraints(2); c.require(3,4); c.require(3,5); constrainedGreedy(6, 1, c)` returns degrees [1,1,0,2,1,1] — vertex 3 has 2 buddies at k=1 — with no error, violating the module header's unconditional "no vertex exceeds k buddies". Larger: `new Constraints(3)` with require(5,6),(5,7),(5,8) and `constrainedGreedy(10, 1, cons)` yields degree(5)=3 at k=1. In dev the only signal is `constrainedGreedy: degree of 5 is 3 > k=1`, a postcondition that blames the callee for a caller precondition that should have fired first. Mechanism: `degreeOf` (constraints.ts:38) allocates `new Array(cons.n)` and does `d[a] += 1` for endpoints >= cons.n, extending the array with holes/NaN instead of refusing; `requiredDegree()` then returns e.g. [0,0,0,null,null,null,null,null,null].
remediation: Close the size-disagreement at its source rather than the one symptom. In `checkWellFormed`, refuse `n !== cons.n` with a clear message (the same rule `Constraints.merge` and `buildConstrainedBuddyGraph` already enforce — the primitive is the only entry point that does not), and make `degreeOf` throw on an endpoint outside [0, n) instead of silently extending the array, so `requiredDegree()`/`prohibitedDegree()` can never return a hole-y vector for any caller. Consider having `polishConstrained`'s `checkConstraintIds(input.n, cons)` apply the same n-agreement rule for consistency.
invariant: For every (n, k, cons), `constrainedGreedy(n, k, cons)` either throws or returns a graph g with `g.degree(v) <= k` for all v, every required pair present and no prohibited pair present — and this must hold with the dev postconditions disabled (NODE_ENV=production). Equivalently at the seam: `constrainedGreedy` throws whenever `n !== cons.n`, and `Constraints.requiredDegree()`/`prohibitedDegree()` never return an array containing a hole or a non-finite entry.

theme: a generation entry point whose only cost gate is a work estimator that can evaluate to zero, with no size cap behind it — so the guard admits every roster size
summary: `repairDegrees` is guarded only by `greedyWork(g.n, k) > MAX_GREEDY_WORK`, and `greedyWork` returns exactly 0 for every k <= 2 at every n (edgesAdded = n*k/2 - n = 0 at k=2), so this exported entry point accepts a graph of any size up to MAX_ROSTER (1e6) and then runs unbounded O(n^2) work.
failure: `repairDegrees(new Graph(n), 2)` (and k=1) on an empty graph: greedyWork(1e6,2) === 0, so the guard passes. Measured wall-clock, clean quadratic: n=5000 -> 1.2 s, n=10000 -> 4.5 s, n=20000 -> 19.7 s, n=40000 -> 76.3 s, all returning 0 edges. Extrapolating the confirmed n^2 curve to the largest n the guard admits (MAX_ROSTER = 1e6) is ~13 hours. Each of the |under| vertices pays one bfsDistances (Int32Array(n) alloc + fill) plus an O(|under|) candidate scan, and with minDist=3 on an empty graph no edge is ever added, so the whole n^2 is spent to accomplish nothing. `ringGreedy` has the identical k=2 hole but is saved by its separate MAX_CACHED_N size cap; `repairDegrees` is the one exported generator in the tree that has a work cap and no size cap, which is exactly the pairing budgets.ts's own module header declares mandatory ("Each generation path needs BOTH a size cap (memory) and a work cap (time)").
remediation: Close it in the estimator so both callers are covered by one change: charge the unavoidable O(n^2) baseline in `greedyWork`, e.g. `3 * n * n * Math.max(edgesAdded, 1)`. This provably does not move ringGreedy's accept-set (for k>=3 edgesAdded is already >= 1, and at k=2 the new value 3n^2 = 7.5e7 at n=5000 stays far inside MAX_GREEDY_WORK), while greedyWork(1e6,2) becomes 3e12 and refuses. Name the sibling before committing: `constrainedWork` is also 0 at k=0, but that path is backed by the MAX_CONSTRAINED_N size cap in both `validate` and `checkWellFormed`, so it is safe — repairDegrees is the only unbacked one. Alternatively/additionally add the missing size cap (`g.n > MAX_CACHED_N` throws) so the doctrine holds structurally rather than relying on the estimator staying positive.
invariant: For every integer k >= 0 and every n > MAX_CACHED_N, `repairDegrees(new Graph(n), k)` throws rather than returning; equivalently, `greedyWork(n, k) > 0` for all n >= 2 and all k >= 0, so no (n, k) can be admitted by a zero-valued work estimate.

theme: a cost budget that does not charge work performed outside the loop it bounds, so the pass costs up to twice its stated budget
summary: `polish`'s anneal temperature calibration runs up to `min(100, max(10, m), maxIters)` full `energy()` evaluations — each an `allPairsSummary`, i.e. the same cost as one loop iteration — but `loopBudget()` only subtracts FIXED_POLISH_SWEEPS = 3 sweeps, whose comment claims to include "the anneal calibration's amortised share". When `maxIters <= 100` (which is precisely the large-n regime the budget exists for) the calibration costs `maxIters` sweeps, not ~1, so the default mode performs ~2x MAX_POLISH_WORK.
failure: `polish(ring(2050))` — boundedPolishIterations returns maxIters = 99 for both modes, and both report iters=99, but measured: mode "hill" 11.4 s, mode "anneal" (the DEFAULT) 24.4 s. The 2.1x delta is entirely the 99 uncharged calibration sweeps. The overshoot is bounded at 2x (calibration <= min(100, maxIters) * perIteration <= loopBudget), so this is a budget-accuracy defect rather than an unbounded hang — but MAX_POLISH_WORK is the constant every other gate in budgets.ts is calibrated against, and on this container 8.65e8 units already measures ~23 s (buildBuddyGraph(120,4), the calibration point itself, took 22.9 s), so 2x is ~46 s on a nominally-bounded default path.
remediation: Charge the calibration where it is spent instead of pretending it is a fixed constant: subtract the calibration's actual sweeps from the loop allowance (compute `trials` first, then run the loop for `maxIters - trials` iterations), or equivalently have `boundedPolishIterations` take the mode and halve the allowance for anneal. Then FIXED_POLISH_SWEEPS drops to the 2 sweeps that really are fixed (starting energy + final summary) and the constant stops overstating what it covers.
invariant: For every (n, m, requested, mode), the total number of `allPairsSummary` evaluations performed by one `polish()` call is at most FIXED_POLISH_SWEEPS + boundedPolishIterations(n, m, requested, DEFAULT_POLISH_ITERS) — in particular the count must not depend on `mode`.

theme: a constructor that materializes O(n^2) state from an attacker-chosen n before any size gate can refuse it
summary: `Constraints.fromTags` never validates `n` — unlike `degreeOf` in the same file, the `Graph` constructor and `validate`, all of which guard it — and then runs an unconditional `for (let i = 0; i < n; i++)` double loop, so both the loop trip count and the prohibited-pair Set are sized by untrusted input before `validate`'s MAX_CONSTRAINED_N refusal can ever run.
failure: Reproduced: `Constraints.fromTags(3e7, [])` completes the empty outer loop in 0.19 s with no guard whatsoever — the loop is O(n) in a value that is only bounded by Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, so `fromTags(1e15, [])` spins for hours. And `Constraints.fromTags(3000, Array(3000).fill('A'))` takes 4.62 s to materialize 4,498,500 prohibited pair keys; at tens of millions of pairs the Set construction itself throws before `validate` gets a chance to refuse. Filed as a DEFERRAL, not blocking, per the reporting contract's mechanical test: `grep -rn fromTags app/src lib/src scripts` returns no caller outside lib/test, so nothing untrusted reaches it in the current tree. This is already recorded in lib/CLAUDE.md's known-limitations with the same measurements; it is re-filed only because the review is full-surface and the finding is real, not to re-litigate the deferral.
remediation: When the tag UI lands (F6): guard `n` against MAX_ROSTER/MAX_CONSTRAINED_N as the first statement, then pre-count group sizes with a single O(n) pass over `tags` and refuse against a pair cap (sum over groups of size*(size-1)/2) BEFORE entering the double loop. Also sanitize tag values — a NaN tag never equals itself, so it silently inverts `prohibit_same`.
invariant: For every n and every tags array, `Constraints.fromTags(n, tags)` either throws before executing any loop iteration, or performs work proportional to n + the number of pairs it actually emits, with that pair count itself refused against a cap before the first `prohibit()` call — i.e. no input can make fromTags do more work than the gate that is supposed to bound it.

theme: the documented checklist for extending the constraint hard-constraint OCP seam omits a real sync point, so a future extender who follows lib/CLAUDE.md literally ships a precondition gap in the exact class of bug that sync point was added to close
summary: lib/CLAUDE.md tells a future implementer of a genuinely-new hard-constraint category to keep four functions in sync — legalEdge, swapBreaksConstraint, assertHardConstraints, and buildReport — but constrainedGreedy.ts's checkInputSatisfiesConstraints (lines 399-416) does the same required/prohibited-pair enumeration as a fifth, undocumented sync point, and the code comment explains it was added for exactly this reason: assertHardConstraints is compiled out in production (dev-only) and previously mis-blamed polishConstrained's caller for a violation polishConstrained could not have introduced. A new hard-constraint category added by touching only the documented four leaves checkInputSatisfiesConstraints blind to it in production.
failure: Add a hypothetical fifth constraint category (e.g. `mustBeAtLeastKApart`) and follow the CLAUDE.md instructions exactly: update legalEdge (so generation respects it), swapBreaksConstraint (so polish swaps respect it), assertHardConstraints (dev-mode postcondition), and buildReport (violation counting). Do NOT touch checkInputSatisfiesConstraints. Then call polishConstrained directly (a documented, supported low-level entry point — 'these are low-level primitives... called directly they throw on malformed input but otherwise assume feasibility') in production (NODE_ENV=production, so CONTRACTS_ENABLED is false) with a hand-built graph that already violates the new category. The precondition that exists specifically to catch this class of defect (a graph arriving already in violation) silently passes, and the swap-only pass can return a 'best' graph that never satisfies the new category, with no error and no signal — the same silent-violation failure mode the comment at line ~149-155 says this check exists to prevent for required/prohibited.
remediation: Add checkInputSatisfiesConstraints to the documented sync list in lib/CLAUDE.md's known-limitations/OCP note, or better: derive its checks from the same iteration legalEdge/swapBreaksConstraint use so a new category can't be added to three of the four/five places and compile cleanly. At minimum, state the fifth touchpoint by name so grep for 'requiredPairs()' — which is what actually finds it — isn't the only way a future implementer discovers it.
invariant: for every function that enumerates cons.requiredPairs()/cons.prohibitedPairs()/cons.isRequired()/cons.isProhibited() to implement a hard-constraint check (found by grep across lib/src), that function's name appears in lib/CLAUDE.md's 'kept in sync' list for a new hard-constraint category — currently 4 of 5 do.

theme: the priorHard flag that promotes soft priors to hard constraints is honoured by exactly one of the several entry points that claim to honour hard constraints, so the feasibility gate and the low-level generators silently disagree with the builder
summary: `validateDetailed`/`validate` and the exported primitives `constrainedGreedy`/`polishConstrained` all ignore `Constraints.priorHard`; only `buildConstrainedBuddyGraph` applies `withHardPriors`, so the documented "authoritative feasibility gate" passes inputs the builder then refuses, and a direct primitive caller gets soft priors where the flag promises hard.
failure:
Reproduced (/home/user/ringweave/.review-scratch/priorhard.mjs).
(a) `const c = new Constraints(6); c.prohibit(0,1); c.addPrior(0,1); c.priorHard = true;` → `validate(c, 3)` returns `[]` (feasible) but `buildConstrainedBuddyGraph(6,3,c).report.refusals` is `["pair 0–1 is both required and prohibited"]`.
(b) priors `[[0,1],[0,2],[0,3]]` with `priorHard = true` → `validate(c2, 2)` returns `[]` but the builder refuses with `["person 0 has 3 required buddies but each person gets 2"]`.
(c) `const c3 = new Constraints(6); c3.addPrior(0,3); c3.priorHard = true;` → `constrainedGreedy(6,2,c3)` returns edges `[[0,1],[0,2],[1,4],[2,3],[3,5],[4,5]]` — `hasEdge(0,3) === false`, i.e. the hard prior is absent; `polishConstrained` then accepts that graph without complaint (its always-on `checkInputSatisfiesConstraints` does not consider promoted priors either), while the builder on the same constraints does produce edge 0–3. A UI that preflights with `validate` (as `app/src/io/feasibility.ts` does) would tell the organizer the roster is feasible and then have generation refuse it — the exact silent preflight/authority disagreement `app/src/constraints.ts` warns about in its own header.
remediation: Close it once, at the promotion seam rather than at each caller: move `withHardPriors` out of `index.ts` and apply it inside `validateDetailed` (which already receives the `Constraints` and can read `priorHard`), and inside `constrainedGreedy`/`polishConstrained`'s precondition path, so all four entry points reason about the same effective constraint set. Sibling to name before committing: `polishConstrained`'s `checkInputSatisfiesConstraints` and `swapBreaksConstraint` must treat promoted priors as required too, or a hard prior can be swapped away by a direct caller. Mirror in `reference-python/constraints.py` `validate` and regenerate fixtures.
invariant: For all n, k and all Constraints c with c.n === n: validate(c, k).length === 0 implies buildConstrainedBuddyGraph(n, k, c).report.refusals.length === 0; and c.priorHard === true implies every pair in c.priorPairs() is an edge of constrainedGreedy(n, k, c) and of polishConstrained(constrainedGreedy(n, k, c), c).

theme: a metric documented as "0 = provably optimal" can report better-than-optimal, because the Moore bound is computed for a degree/size combination in which no connected graph exists
summary: `mooreLowerBounds(n, 1)` for n ≥ 3 returns a positive `asplLb` derived from a Moore tree that no max-degree-1 graph can realise (a matching is the best possible and is disconnected), so `asplGap` returns a NEGATIVE gap — "better than provably optimal" — for the honest within-group ASPL, and `diameterLb` is likewise above anything achievable.
failure:
Reproduced (/home/user/ringweave/.review-scratch/moore.mjs). The best max-degree-1 graph on n vertices is a perfect matching, whose within-group `allPairsSummary().aspl` is exactly 1:
  n=3 k=1: asplLb 1.5000, diameterLb 2 → asplGap(1,3,1) = -0.3333
  n=4 k=1: asplLb 1.6667, diameterLb 2 → asplGap(1,4,1) = -0.4000
  n=7 k=1: asplLb 1.8333, diameterLb 2 → asplGap(1,7,1) = -0.4545
The function's own docstring reserves the `{asplLb: 0, diameterLb: 0}` "no bound" signal for k ≤ 0 / n ≤ 1, but k=1 with n ≥ 3 is equally degenerate — no connected graph with max degree 1 exists there at all. Verified mirrored in `reference-python/core.py` (`moore_lower_bounds(3,1) == (1.5, 2)`), so a fix has to go through the oracle. The existing ratchet does not catch it: `optimizer.props.test.ts:538` only asserts `diameterLb <= n - 1`, and its comment ("A k-regular graph on n vertices always exists for some parity") is false for k=1, n ≥ 3. No live caller reaches the negative value today — `buildBuddyGraph` always returns a connected graph and `app/src/model.ts assembleMetrics` gates `quality` on `connected` — which is why this is a suggestion rather than blocking; it is a latent recurrence of the "a split roster scores optimal" theme this repo has already been burned by.
remediation: Extend the degenerate-input guard in `mooreLowerBounds` to every (n, k) for which no connected graph with max degree ≤ k exists — i.e. also `k === 1 && n > 2` — returning the existing `{asplLb: 0, diameterLb: 0}` "no bound" signal so `asplGap` yields 0 rather than a negative number. Change `reference-python/core.py moore_lower_bounds` first, regenerate `reference.json`, then mirror. Replace the `diameterLb <= n - 1` assertion with the invariant below so the property, not the k=1 case, is what is ratcheted.
invariant: For all integers n ≥ 0 and k ≥ 0 and every Graph g on n vertices with max degree ≤ k: if allPairsSummary(g).aspl is finite then mooreLowerBounds(n, k).asplLb <= allPairsSummary(g).aspl and mooreLowerBounds(n, k).diameterLb <= allPairsSummary(g).diameter — equivalently, asplGap(allPairsSummary(g).aspl, n, k) >= 0 for every such g.

theme: a bounded budget is spent entirely on setup, buys zero of the work it was granted for, and the result is still reported as done
summary: The anneal temperature calibration is capped by `maxIters` and then subtracted from it, so any iteration budget of 100 or less leaves `loopIters === 0`: polish pays the full budget in `energy()` sweeps, performs no accept/reject decision, returns the input byte-identical, and `buildBuddyGraph` still reports `polished: true`.
failure: `trials = Math.min(100, Math.max(10, edges.length), maxIters)` then `loopIters = Math.max(0, maxIters - calibrationSweeps)` gives 0 for every maxIters in [1,100]. Reproduced: `polish(ring(200), {mode:"anneal", maxIters: 100})` -> `iters: 0`, output edge list identical to input, 110 ms burned. Reachable straight through the public builder because `boundedPolishIterations` returns <= 100 whenever n*(n+m) >= 8.32e6: `buildBuddyGraph(3000, 2, {polish:true})` takes 7054 ms against 572 ms for `{polish:false}` (12.3x) and returns a byte-identical edge list with `polished: true` and identical `aspl`; `buildBuddyGraph(1700, 4, {polish:true})` 32464 ms vs 19906 ms; `buildBuddyGraph(316, 315, {polish:true})` 12256 ms vs 5715 ms. The guard that should have stopped this is the very fix that created it: `lib/test/optimizer.props.test.ts:491` ("charges the anneal calibration against the same budget as the loop") only exercises `maxIters: 0`, so the case where the calibration takes 100% of a POSITIVE budget is untested, and index.ts:178 sets `polished = true` from the fact that `polish` was called rather than from `PolishResult.iters`.
remediation: Give the calibration a bounded FRACTION of the budget instead of the whole of it (e.g. `trials = Math.min(100, Math.max(10, edges.length), Math.floor(maxIters / 2))`), and skip anneal calibration entirely (falling back to hill acceptance or the 0.1 default T0) when the budget cannot afford both calibration and at least one loop iteration. Close the sibling in the same change: derive `BuddyResult.polished` from `PolishResult.iters > 0` rather than from having called `polish`, so the flag cannot claim work that did not happen.
invariant: For every graph g with at least 2 edges and every requested budget for which `boundedPolishIterations` returns i >= 1, `polish(g, {mode:"anneal", maxIters: i}).iters >= 1` — a positive iteration budget always buys at least one optimization iteration, in both modes. And for all (n, k, options), `BuddyResult.polished === true` implies the polish pass performed at least one accept/reject decision, i.e. `polished` is never true while the returned edge list is identical to the pre-polish graph's for reasons of budget.

theme: a non-finite numeric option silently changes an algorithm's semantics instead of being refused
summary: `repairDegrees` validates `k` but not `minDist`, so a NaN or negative separation floor makes `distv[v] < minDist` false for every vertex, silently disabling the separation constraint and producing a different graph — the exact failure mode the same file's comments say was closed for `mind` here and for `priorWeight` in the constrained polish.
failure: `repairDegrees(ring(20), 4, NaN)` returns a graph with girth 3 and 40 edges; `repairDegrees(ring(20), 4, 3)` (the documented default) returns girth 4 and 39 edges. `-Infinity` and `-5` behave identically to NaN. `repairDegrees` is exported public API (its own doc block says so explicitly and lists this failure mode for `k`), and `minDist` is its only numeric parameter with no guard. The result is a silently WRONG graph — triangles where the caller asked for a distance-3 floor — not an ignored option.
remediation: Guard `minDist` in the same statement style as `k` at the top of `repairDegrees`: throw on `!Number.isInteger(minDist) || minDist < 0`. This is a one-line subtraction of a hole, not a new abstraction, and it makes the three numeric options of the greedy path (`k`, `mind`, `minDist`) uniformly refusing.
invariant: For every exported entry point in lib/src/core, every numeric option that participates in a comparison is refused (throws, or refuses via `Reason`) when it is not a non-negative integer — no such value may produce output that differs from the output for the documented default. Concretely: for all graphs g, all valid k, and all md with `!Number.isInteger(md) || md < 0`, `repairDegrees(g, k, md)` throws.

theme: a size gate runs after the O(m) materialization it is supposed to bound
summary: `polishConstrained` derives `m` from `input.edgeList()` — which allocates m two-element arrays and sorts them — and only then calls `checkPolishSize`, so the refusal path pays O(m log m) time and O(m) memory; `polish` deliberately derives the same `m` from the O(n) degree sum precisely to avoid this.
failure: `polishConstrained(ring(1_000_000), new Constraints(1_000_000), {iters: 0})` refuses in 150 ms after materializing and sorting 1e6 pair arrays, while `polish(ring(1_000_000), {maxIters: 0})` refuses the same graph in 41 ms without allocating anything m-sized. The cost is unbounded in m: `Graph` places no cap on edge count, so a denser input scales the pre-refusal allocation linearly with no gate in front of it. polish.ts:60 carries the comment explaining exactly why the cheap derivation was chosen there; the constrained sibling was not brought along. The two O(#constraints) precondition scans (`checkConstraintIds` spreads all three pair arrays into one new array) sit in front of the gate for the same reason.
remediation: In `polishConstrained`, compute `m` the way `polish` does (`input.degrees().reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) / 2`) and call `checkPolishSize` before `input.edgeList()`, `checkConstraintIds` and `checkInputSatisfiesConstraints`. Better still, extract the one derivation both entry points use so the two cannot drift again.
invariant: In every polish entry point, `checkPolishSize` is reached without executing any allocation or sort proportional to the edge count: `m` is derived from the degree sum (O(n)), and `edgeList()` is never called on a graph the size gate would refuse.

theme: a work budget's units are not rate-comparable across the shapes it admits, so its accept-set contains calls far past its documented wall-clock ceiling
summary: `MAX_GREEDY_WORK` (1.5e10) admits a 114-second single synchronous call: `greedyWork`'s `max(edgesAdded, 1)` floor prices `repairDegrees`'s O(n^2) per-vertex-BFS sweep in the same units as ringGreedy's cache updates, which run roughly 4x faster per unit.
failure: `repairDegrees(new Graph(70710), 2)` measured 113752 ms. It is admitted exactly: `greedyWork(70710, 2) = 3 * 70710^2 * max(0, 70710*2/2 - 70710 -> 1) = 1.5e10 = MAX_GREEDY_WORK`. For comparison the same budget number at a dense shape costs far less — `buildBuddyGraph(1000, 12)` (greedyWork 1.5e10) is 30.8 s and `buildBuddyGraph(316, 315)` (1.48e10) is 5.9 s — so one budget number buys wall clocks spanning 19x, and the constant's own comment states "1e10 is therefore ~60 s worst case" while the constant shipped is 1.5e10. n=70710 is the exact peak: k=2 is the only degree that engages the `edgesAdded -> 1` floor, and k>=3 drives n below 2155 where the same sweep is trivial. Not reachable from untrusted input in the current tree (no app caller for `repairDegrees`; `ringGreedy`'s internal call is bounded by MAX_CACHED_N=5000), but it is live exported API of a published package.
remediation: Charge the sweep in the units it actually costs rather than papering over it with a floor: when `edgesAdded` is 0, `repairDegrees` still performs n `bfsDistances` calls each allocating and filling an `Int32Array(n)`, so the floor term should be scaled to that per-BFS cost — or `repairDegrees` should carry its own n cap, as `ringGreedy` does with MAX_CACHED_N, instead of relying solely on a work model calibrated on a different shape. Whichever is chosen, restate the constant's wall-clock ceiling from the value actually shipped.

theme: a numeric option meant only to ever help an objective (a soft-penalty weight) has no sign guard, so a negative value silently makes the optimizer actively fight the goal it names, with no error and no visible signal beyond a suspiciously low reported fraction
summary: `priorWeight` on `polishConstrained`/`buildConstrainedBuddyGraph` (the exact knob F9's 'preserve current buddies' toggle drives) is only finiteness-checked (`Number.isFinite(opts.priorWeight)`), never sign-checked. `constrainedMeasure` (line 362) computes `energy += priorWeight * (priors.length - countPresentEdges(g, priors))`: with a negative weight, breaking a prior edge *lowers* the objective, so the swap-polish optimizer is rewarded for destroying prior buddies rather than preserving them — the exact inverse of the documented contract ('Soft penalty weight for keeping prior buddies'). The codebase has already hardened this exact option against the sibling failure (NaN silently disabling the penalty, per the comment at greedy.ts:210) but not against negative values silently inverting it, which is worse: NaN produces a visible no-op, this produces active, silent harm.
failure: Reproduced directly against the built lib/dist: 10-person roster, one new person joins, previous edges added as priors on the new 11-person roster, `buildConstrainedBuddyGraph(11, 4, cons, {priorWeight: 2})` reports `priorsKeptFraction: 0.947`; the identical call with `priorWeight: -5` reports `priorsKeptFraction: 0`. No throw, no refusal entry, `report.satisfied` is unaffected (priors are not part of the hard-constraint satisfied check) — a caller reading only `satisfied` sees nothing wrong.
remediation: Guard `priorWeight` the same way `mind`/`k` are guarded elsewhere in this file: reject (throw, matching the direct-call contract of `polishConstrained`) or clamp negative values to 0 in both `polishConstrained` (constrainedGreedy.ts:172) and `buildConstrainedBuddyGraph`'s resolution (index.ts:358-359), and extend the existing property test (`constrained.props.test.ts`'s 'a higher prior weight never keeps fewer priors than zero weight') to sweep negative weights so the invariant is ratcheted rather than re-discovered.
invariant: for all real priorWeight < 0 passed to polishConstrained/buildConstrainedBuddyGraph, the number of prior pairs present in the output graph must be >= the number present when priorWeight = 0 (i.e., a negative weight must never be honoured as a preservation instruction — it must be refused or clamped, never applied as-is).

theme: False numerical claims in comments mislead contributors searching for code scope
summary: Comment claims DEFAULT_MIN_SEPARATION is shared by 'three generation entry points' but only two exist
failure: A contributor searching for all usages of DEFAULT_MIN_SEPARATION, expecting to find three sites as the comment states, will look for a third and get confused when only two exist (buildBuddyGraph and ringGreedy). buildConstrainedBuddyGraph accepts but ignores the constant.
remediation: Change the comment from 'Shared so the three generation entry points can't drift apart' to 'Shared so the two generation entry points can't drift apart', or remove the count entirely. Verify: grep -n 'DEFAULT_MIN_SEPARATION' lib/src/core/*.ts shows usage at exactly 2 sites (greedy.ts:54 and index.ts:164).
invariant: DEFAULT_MIN_SEPARATION is used as a default value in exactly two entry points (buildBuddyGraph at index.ts:164 and ringGreedy at greedy.ts:54), not three
